Proposed deal would combine complementary networks, spectrum and operating capabilities
Quebecor has made a proposal worth $31 billion to take over Telus.

The telecom company said Monday in a news release it submitted a non-binding proposal to Telus in June to serve as a basis for negotiations. Telus is currently reviewing an enhanced proposal submitted by Quebecor earlier this month, according to the release.
The Montreal-based company says the proposed deal would combine complementary networks, spectrum and operating capabilities to strengthen investment capacity and competitive positioning.
Quebecor, Canada's fourth largest telecom company, argues that acquiring Telus would create a stronger company that could better serve consumers across the country.

"This proposal will create a strong pan-Canadian competitor, able to compete on equal terms with the other national providers and to stand up to foreign companies, for the benefit of Canadians," Quebecor said in the statement.

articles.title: Under-threat lidos get lifeline as Andy Burnham sets up fund to rebuild pools
articles.summary:
Move reflects growing demand for outdoor swimming as Britain heats up and follows campaign by MPs

Andy Burnham is setting up a public fund to rebuild the UK’s lidos after a revival in…

blocks.text: Andy Burnham is setting up a public fund to rebuild the UK’s lidos after a revival in outdoor swimming.
Outdoor pools were built across the UK in the 1930s. The often beautiful, art deco constructions were made as a cheap way to provide access to healthy activity during the summer.

In the following decades the lidos fell into decline and by the end of the 1980s nearly two-thirds were derelict or demolished. Britain had more than 300 lidos in the 1930s but only about a third were still open in 1990. Some survivors are still at risk of closing down today and communities are fighting to keep them open.
Now, the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport has committed to creating a dedicated national fund to reinvigorate the UK’s lidos, after a campaign by MPs.

The move reflects the growing demand for outdoor swimming as summers in Britain heat up, and the fact that many communities do not have a place for cooling off. Better, the biggest leisure centre group in the country, which runs 10 outdoor swimming centres, said 2026 was by far its busiest year for outdoor swimming, with trips to its lidos between June and August rising by 28% to 692,471 visits.
Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, said the investment would be “the first dedicated fund for lidos that this country has produced” and would form part of a wider public leisure facilities programme.
MPs who have campaigned to keep lidos open in their cities welcomed news of the fund.
Andrew Pakes, the Labour MP for Peterborough, who campaigned to keep the city’s lido open after the council’s budget plans suggested it could be mothballed, said the announcement was welcome news.

This year, Peterborough’s Grade II-listed art deco lido celebrated its 90th anniversary and its best ever season, which Pakes said echoed the experience at outdoor swimming facilities in many other cities. “This makes protecting and supporting our pools even more important,” he said.
after newsletter promotion

He has been leading a group of MPs who have been calling for funding to build or reopen lidos in their local areas. “For places like Peterborough, the lido is far more than somewhere to swim. It is a much-loved part of our city’s heritage, bringing people together across generations,” he said.

The Carlisle MP, Julie Minns, who founded the campaign to save the city’s Grade II-listed Victorian and Turkish Baths, said: “These are places that bring communities together, support physical and mental wellbeing and form an important part of our shared heritage. In Carlisle, our Victorian and Turkish Baths are one of the city’s most distinctive historic buildings and have served generations of local residents.”

articles.title: International student enrollments at US universities plunge this fall, data shows
articles.summary:
Report finds fewer international students studying in US amid Trump’s crackdowns on immigration and education

Fewer international students are studying at

blocks.text: Fewer international students are studying at US universities as the Trump administration cracks down on immigration and reshapes higher education, data released on Monday show.

Overall, US campuses saw a 9% decrease in international enrollment this fall compared with last year, according to a survey from the Institute of International Education. And the number of new students entering the United States for the first time fell by 15%.

“No one aspires to send their kids to get educated in the US,” said Veena Dubal, general counsel for the American Association of University Professors, whose father traveled from India to attend Tuskegee University, then the Tuskegee Institute, in the late 1960s on a student visa.
“It feels like an unsafe place. That’s the message that the Trump administration has been sending to families all over the world and they’re listening.”

Last year, the enrollment decreases were partially offset by large numbers of students who stayed in the US for temporary work after graduating. But after months of speculation, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) proposed requiring schools to pay a $70,000 fee for every student who participates in the optional practice training program.
Although the rule hasn’t been finalized, participation in the program, known as OPT for short, dropped 6% this fall, according to the survey.

The proposed rule, which is expected to face legal challenges, is part of wider DHS efforts that include terminating the legal status of thousands of international students, along with detaining and deporting many of them.

And this summer, the administration finalized a rule that will prevent international students from staying in the US for more than four years without approval from the federal government, although a judge has temporarily blocked it.
DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin has said the changes were intended to crack down on loopholes that international students were exploiting by extending their studies.
Although the US remains the top destination for international students globally, the changes are having an effect, college leaders told the IIE.

Among more than 800 US colleges and universities surveyed this fall, 88% blamed the visa application process and 70% blamed travel restrictions for the enrollment drops. And if OPT options are limited, 95% of schools predicted that international students would probably look to another country, according to the survey, which offers an early look at trends before full data is released next year.

Politics aren’t the only reason students are looking elsewhere, said Mirka Martel, head of research, evaluation and learning for the institute. Its survey found more global competition for international students and the rising cost of a US degree also contributed.

Fanta Aw, the executive director and CEO of Nafsa, an association that represents international education, said students also are worried about research funding. Last year, the Trump administration began dismantling the federal grant-giving process and attempting to exert more political influence over what projects get funded.

“They’re saying to themselves: ‘Too much uncertainty in the United States. It’s too difficult, and you know, more importantly, we have many more choices today than we did 10 years ago. Why subject ourselves to this?’” Aw said, noting that students are going to places like China.

Nafsa, in partnership with the international education technology company JB International, found that amid the enrollment decline, international students’ contributions to the US economy dropped by $2.4bn this fall.
US colleges and universities heavily recruit students from overseas as a source of tuition revenue. So the drops have punched big holes in tuition revenue at some schools.

At Cleveland State University, international enrollment has dropped by 46% in two years, from 1,542 in fall 2025 to 828 this fall. And fewer than 50 new international students started this fall, said provost Nigamanth Sridhar, who estimated that the budgetary impact ranges from $2m to $4m.
Decades ago, he arrived in the US on an F1 student visa and participated in OPT. Eventually, he went through the process to become a naturalized citizen.

“I am here in this position, in this job, because I had the opportunity to come to the United States as an international graduate student and then decided to stay here and build a career,” said Sridhar, who is from India. “So international education is personal to me.”

The biggest drops were at the graduate level. This fall’s data shows a 15% drop in international graduate enrollment, compared to a 3% decrease at the undergraduate level. The report also found declines in international students from India, which sends more students to the US to study than any other country.

Sarah Spreitzer, vice-president at the American Council on Education, which represents college and university presidents, said substantial immigration bills are unlikely while Donald Trump remains president. But she said congressional oversight after Trump’s Republican party suffered big losses in the 3 November midterms might halt new policies targeted at international students.
“Those types of things could provide more certainty for our international students that there’s not just going to be these sudden or unexplainable changes,” Spreitzer said.

articles.title: USC star JuJu Watkins could change Toronto Tempo's future, providing she declares for WNBA draft
articles.summary: Most WNBA executives have long considered JuJu Watkins a generational prospect, a player potentially on par with A’Ja Wilson, Cailtin Clark or Paige Bueckers as far as altering a franchise's future.

image.caption: USC star JuJu Watkins is the consensus No. 1 pick for next year's WNBA draft, though she has yet to declare herself eligible. (Ethan Miller/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Basketball·Analysis
Most WNBA executives have long considered JuJu Watkins a generational prospect, a player potentially on par with A’Ja Wilson, Cailtin Clark or Paige Bueckers as far as altering a franchise's future.
A generational prospect, 21-year-old wants to win NCAA title before turning pro
· for CBC Sports
· Posted: Nov 16, 2026 8:32 AM EST | Last Updated: 26 minutes ago

If you want a glimpse into the future of the WNBA, we encourage you to watch highlights from Sunday’s women’s college basketball game between the University of South Carolina and the University of Southern California. The game was marketed as “The Real SC” (both teams use “SC” as part of their athletic identity) but calling it The WNBA Draft Invitational would have been more accurate.

There were future first-round picks all across Bon Secours Wellness Arena in Greenville, S.C., including a six-pack of prospects from No. 1-ranked South Carolina (Joyce Edwards, Chloe Kitts, Tessa Johnson, Agot Makeer, Jerzy Robinson and Ashlyn Watkins). The No. 3-ranked USC star contingent included sophomore guards Jazzy Davidson, Kennedy Smith and freshman forward-guard Saniyah Hall, the top-ranked high school recruit entering the season. All of the players above are projected as first-round picks between the 2027 and 2029 WNBA drafts.

But in a game featuring future WNBA stars, there was one prospect who stood above the rest as far as name recognition and possibility — USC guard-forward JuJu Watkins, a six-foot-two senior wing with the ability to score from three levels (at the rim, mid-range and three-point distance). Most WNBA executives have long considered Watkins a generational prospect, a player potentially on par with A’Ja Wilson, Cailtin Clark or Paige Bueckers as far as altering a franchise's future.

On Sunday, the 21-year-old Watkins showed flashes of what she can be. She has one of the most artistically pleasing pull-up jumpers in the history of women’s college basketball and unlike many prolific scorers, she attacks defences with the intensity of a starving pit bull. You win titles in the WNBA with elite front-court players and Watkins can swing seamlessly between the forward and guard spots, making her a difficult challenge for defences. Her potential is vast — she missed the entire 2025–26 season due to a torn right ACL and looks like she has not missed a beat. But the complete product is still a couple of years away. Watkins finished with 25 points on 8 of 20 shooting against South Carolina but also had five turnovers. (South Carolina’s big-game experience and deeper frontcourt talent was the difference; they held on for an 89-85 win.)

Like most WNBA executives, Toronto Tempo general manager Monica Wright Rogers watched Sunday afternoon’s game very closely. But Wright Rogers had far more stake than most. The Tempo entered Sunday night’s WNBA lottery with a 32.9 per cent chance at the No. 1 pick in the 2027 draft, tied with the Houston Comets (formerly the Connecticut Sun) for the best odds .
By now you likely know what happened: Toronto landed the No. 1 pick.

items: Toronto Tempo earn No. 1 pick after winning 2027 WNBA draft lottery

blocks.text: ANEESAH CALLED IT 🇨🇦 Morrow had a feeling tonight would be special, and @TempoBasketball is walking away with the No. 1 overall pick! WNBA Draft Lottery 2027 | @StateStreetETFs SPY https://t.co/bPtvhbcgF5—WNBA

“There were no words for the emotion that filled our conference room where I was with the strategy team and our comms [communication] team,” Rogers said when asked what it was like when she saw the news on television. “Our hearts were beating out of our chest.”

One of the unique twists to the WNBA draft puzzle this year is that the top draft-eligible players in women’s college basketball can all return for another year in college because of the NCAA's new "5-in-5" eligibility rule which allows Division I and II women's basketball players up to five years of eligibility to compete in five seasons. Thus, Watkins has the option for a fifth year at USC as a medical redshirt given she missed last season with an ACL injury. Texas forward Madison Booker, Notre Dame point guard Hannah Hidalgo and LSU’s Mikaylah Williams — the consensus group right behind Watkins — can also choose to return to their American colleges.

“It makes draft planning even tougher for teams and GMs,” said Rebecca Lobo, the Naismith Basketball Hall of Famer who called South Carolina-USC for ESPN. "If JuJu Watkins enters the draft, the impact would be immense both on and off the court for Toronto. She is the type of talent you build a franchise around. Not only an incredible player but she already has a big brand that will help drive ticket sales and viewers. JuJu could be a massive cornerstone for the Tempo.”
Watkins (12) has said she wants to win a NCAA title with her hometown USC before she turns pro. (Melina Pizano/Getty Images)

Where does Watkins stand? Well, the only thing she has offered publicly is that she won’t address her draft status until after USC’s season has concluded. Watkins is L.A.-born and she has repeatedly said her dream is to win a college title in her hometown.

Wright Rogers said on Sunday night that the Tempo front office is in constant communication with college coaches and agents and that will clearly be the case here. Watkins is represented by Klutch Sports Group, which is the agency that also represents NBA star LeBron James.

“Now that we have some direction, we really can hone in on understanding the plan that these athletes have for their future,” Wright Rogers said. “It’s going to be very complicated and it may come down to the wire. Each player has about 48 hours after their last NCAA game to declare. We will stay proactively locked in.”

items: Women's pro sport drives interest for Canadian girls, not necessarily participation, report says

blocks.text: The positives for Watkins to come out in 2027 are what you’d expect. She can compete against the best players in the world, the WNBA is a better launching pad for a shot at the U.S. Olympic team, and playing in Canada will give her the opportunity to market herself not just to a city but an entire country

But here is where it gets tricky. Watkins is a high-profile U.S. college athlete and already has significant Name, Image, and Likeness (NIL) deals with companies such as Nike, Gatorade, and Fanatics. Her 2026 college earnings will almost unquestionably top what she would earn in salary in the WNBA next season. (The salary for the 2027 WNBA No. 1 pick could be as high as $565,000 for next year’s top pick under the new collective bargaining agreement.) Staying in college will continue to make her wealthy.

There is also this: Watkins and her management team might want to place her in a U.S. market. They could roll the dice that her hometown L.A. Sparks (who next season have their own pick as well as the Chicago Sky’s pick) crash out and land the No. 1 pick in the 2028 draft.
Madison Booker (35) is another top prospect the Tempo will be watching. (Christian Petersen/Getty Images)

The good news is the Tempo are likely to land an all-star calibre prospect even if Watkins declines to come out. Booker is a 6-foot-1 forward who can efficiently score from both mid-range and the perimeter — the kind of player that wins you championships. She can defend power forwards given her strength in the post. So far this season she is averaging 21 points per game on 57 per cent shooting. It is very unlikely she will return to Texas.

Hidalgo is one of the best point guard prospects in years, an insanely prolific scorer and a disruptive player on defence who broke the NCAA Division I single-season steals record last season with 202. Her only flaw is size – she’s just 5-foot-7. But so far bigger guards have been unable to stop her. She is averaging an obscene 28.3 points, 7.5 rebounds, 5.5 assists and 4.8 steals this season. LSU’s Williams (a 6-foot guard with a very quick release) is probably next on the list. It is still a very deep draft if everyone opts to come out outside of Watkins.
“Throughout the history of this league, getting the number one pick does alter the trajectory of your franchise,” Wright Rogers said.

There was a significant fiscal commitment from Tempo ownership to be competitive in 2026 — Toronto made Marina Mabrey and Brittany Sykes the league’s first million-dollar backcourt — but things unraveled quickly. The team was ravaged by injuries, finishing at 11-33 including losing 22 of their last 24 games. How bad did it get? The Tempo ranked first overall in games lost to in-season injuries and the quartet of Sykes, Mabrey, Nyara Sabally, and Kiki Rice — the team’s most talented players— played a total of just 78 minutes together this season.

“We are putting in the work to ensure that we don't have the situation with injuries again,” Wright Rogers said. “We're putting in a lot of time reshaping our health and performance group, putting a microscope under the group, and putting resources and the backing into that space so we won't be repeating those same injury woes that we had last season.”

items: 'Only up from here': Tempo's off-court success offers optimism after injury-ravaged inaugural campaign

blocks.text: Toronto currently has six players under contract for 2027 (Mabrey, Sykes, Kiki Rice, Julie Allemand, Aneesah Morrow and Teonni Key) and more than $4 million available in cap space. The No. 1 pick gives them roster construction options and also offers the enticement for free agents to play with a potential franchise player.

Wright Rogers did not formally say that she would pick Watkins during a post-lottery call with reporters if Watkins declares for the pros, but the Tempo boss most certainly will call her name if the star comes out. Given all of this, here is the one bit of advice we can offer as we enter the beginning of JuJu Watch:
If you are a fan of the Toronto Tempo, you should root very hard for the USC Trojans to win the NCAA women’s basketball title next spring.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Richard Deitsch is a Toronto-based writer and podcaster who previously worked for The Athletic as a media reporter as well as Sports Illustrated, where he covered seven Olympic Games among other assignments. He has also worked in radio and was an adjunct professor at Columbia University. He hosts “The Sports Media Podcast,” featuring U.S. and Canadian sports media figures.
With files from The Associated Press

articles.title: Beckham firm sues after fragrance found for sale in Poundland
articles.summary: Brand reacted with ‘shock and dismay’ after products were also found in a ‘bargain bin inside a gas station’

blocks.text: David Beckham’s company reacted with “shock and dismay” after discovering his branded fragrance range was on sale in petrol stations and in Poundland, court documents have revealed.
The former England football captain’s brand, DB Ventures, has launched a lawsuit against the distributor of the products, arguing it allowed them to be sold in stores that had not been agreed upon.

DB Ventures claimed to have discovered the perfumes for sale in the troubled UK budget retailer and in a “bargain bin inside a gas station” at an unspecified location, according to court papers filed in New York.
Lawyers acting for Beckham’s company said it reflected “desperation and greed” by the perfume company, Coty.

Coty, which is headquartered in the Netherlands, has worked with Beckham’s brand for more than a decade and has produced more than 30 different fragrances bearing his name. In the UK, they sell at about £20 per bottle.
Lawyers claimed that Coty sold at least $24m (£18m) of Beckham products through “unapproved distribution channels”.

In the court filing, they said: “DB Ventures, the licensor of the David Beckham brand, ensures that all of its brand licensing partnerships maintain the lifestyle and luxury image of the brand that Sir David has carefully cultivated for decades.

“Imagine, then, the shock and dismay experienced when DB Ventures discovered that David Beckham products were being offered for sale in a gas station. How could this possibly have happened? Desperation and greed.”

The legal documents, filed at the supreme court in New York and first reported by the Daily Mail, allege that Coty had “distributed David Beckham fragrances through the budget retailer Poundland, allowing the product to be sold for dollar store prices and associating the David Beckham brand with cheap, discount products.”
The lawyers asked for compensation and damages totalling $41m. They also claimed Coty under-reported net sales by $123m, which would mean that DB Ventures lost $6m in unpaid royalties.

Coty filed its defence, asking for the case to be dismissed. It denied that it had ever sold the fragrances in Poundland, but argued that it had the right to decide where it wanted to sell its David Beckham range.
after newsletter promotion

Beckham, who retired from professional football in 2013, has built a multimillion-pound business empire, DRJB Holdings, around his brand. The group is made up of three divisions, the largest of which is DB Ventures, which covers most of his commercial partnerships with brands such as Hugo Boss.

The Seven Global division contains licensing agreements with companies such as Adidas, and the remainder of the business is Studio 99, the production studio that made Netflix documentaries about the lives of himself and of his wife, the former Spice Girl and fashion designer Victoria Beckham.

This year David Beckham received a $51m dividend from the group, after a series of lucrative brand deals for the Fifa World Cup. He appeared in about a dozen ad campaigns during the tournament this summer, working with brands such as Lenovo, McDonald’s and Bank of America.
The Beckhams are together worth an estimated £1.2bn, according to the most recent Sunday Times Rich List.
DB Ventures and Coty were approached for comment.

articles.title: US basketball player arrested with 75lb of marijuana at Nigerian airport, say authorities
articles.summary:
• Suspect named as Greene Da’monte Khiree

  • Drug smuggling carries life sentence in Nigeria

An American basketball player has been arrested in Nigeria for…

blocks.text: An American basketball player has been arrested in Nigeria for allegedly attempting to smuggle 33.95kg (75lb) of marijuana into the country.

Nigeria’s National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) said a 28-year-old player it named as Greene Da’monte Khiree from the state of Georgia was arrested at Lagos’s main airport last Wednesday after he arrived on a flight from Thailand via the United Arab Emirates.

The NDLEA said the player told them he had come to Nigeria to “build networks” for his basketball career. The agency said evidence on his phone suggested he had “knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity”. The NDLEA said it detained the player when he attempted to leave the airport with his hand luggage after abandoning two checked-in bags. The agency said those two bags were found to contain 32 parcels of marijuana, and a tracking device.
Nigeria has strict drug laws, and trafficking carries a sentence of life in prison.

A basketball player by the name of Damonte Greene is listed on the roster of the Pattani Raptors in the Thai Premier Men’s League. Greene, a Georgia native, played college basketball for Reinhardt University and South Georgia Technical College. He played semi-professional basketball in the US before representing a number of teams in Thailand.

WNBA star Brittney Griner and former Utah State player Jarred Shaw were imprisoned in Russia and Indonesia respectively for marijuana offenses. Griner was released in December 2022, while Shaw remains in prison.

During the summit’s closing ceremony, the Philippines will also turn over the ASEAN chairmanship to Singapore, which will lead the bloc in 2027.

articles.title: Ministry of Justice investigating Russell Brand message from prison claiming he is not guilty
articles.summary:
PM’s spokesperson calls message, read out by convicted rapist’s wife on their YouTube channel, ‘clearly appalling’

The Ministry of Justice has launched an investigation into whether Russell…

blocks.text: The Ministry of Justice has launched an investigation into whether Russell Brand has broken prison rules after the jailed comedian shared a message claiming he is not guilty of sexual offences just days after his conviction.
Brand’s wife, Laura Brand, read a message from her rapist husband in a video uploaded to their YouTube channel in which he claimed: “I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for.”
It is understood a prisoner will be deemed to have broken the rules if they provide comments to a family member they know will be published.
Any inquiry could also examine whether the current rules need to be updated to stop comments from prisoners being broadcast via profit-making YouTube channels.

Asked about the comments, the prime minister’s official spokesperson said: “This is clearly appalling and is being urgently investigated. We expect action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules. Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances.
“Prisoners cannot get around these rules by having someone else publish their comments … This is being urgently investigated. We expect action to be taken if the rules have been broken.”
Brand, 51, is serving a 10-and-a-half-year prison term after he was convicted of one count of rape and three sexual assaults at Southwark crown court on 5 November.

In his message, Brand said he had been moved from the category B Wandsworth prison in south-west London to the lower category C HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire – a prison for men convicted of sexual offences.
Reading the message from a notebook, Laura Brand said: “As you know, I am not guilty for the offences I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening.”

His message added: “I am incarcerated in HMP Littlehey, little as in small, and hey as in hey, I’m in the biggest sex offenders’ prison in Europe. The good news is that I have already seen that the staff here are strong, they are kind, and they are dedicated. And as for my fellow prisoners, I now know that I am in no position to judge anyone.

“I don’t know which other men here are not guilty, and the ones that are, they are people that Christ died to save, like you and me, let us all love, pray for, and forgive one another as God forgave us.”

Responding to the video on Monday, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, told Sky News: “His crimes are heinous and awful. I think it’s revolting, by the way, that he shows no remorse today in his comments. No remorse, no sympathy for the victims. Just disgusting comments.”
According to official guidance, prisoners are expected to make a formal application through their governor if they wish to contact the media.

Prison sources said current rules may have to be updated to stop people from releasing comments on YouTube channels through which a prisoner or their family may profit via sponsorship or advertising. The rules say: “Correspondence which is intended for publication or for use by radio or television or for posting on the internet (or which if sent, would be likely to be published or broadcast) must not contain material which is for publication in return for payment (unless the prisoner is unconvicted).”

articles.title: Ukraine launches biggest drone attack on Russia since war began: Defence ministry
articles.summary: Russian air defences intercepted 1,336 drones launched by Ukraine, Russia's Defence Ministry said Monday, in what appeared to be Kyiv's biggest aerial attack since Moscow's all-out invasion of its…

image.caption: Russian President Vladimir Putin listens to Russian Transport Minister Dmitry Yadrov at the Kremlin in Moscow on Monday. Ukraine has launched its biggest overnight drone attack on Russia since the full-scale war began in 2022, Russia's Defence Ministry said Monday. (Alexander Kazakov/Sputnik/The Ass

blocks.text: World·New

Russian air defences intercepted 1,336 drones launched by Ukraine, Russia's Defence Ministry said Monday, in what appeared to be Kyiv's biggest aerial attack since Moscow's all-out invasion of its neighbour nearly five years ago.
Russian air defences intercepted some 1,336 drones launched by Ukraine
Ukraine has scaled up its long-range aerial assaults on Russia, as well as illegally annexed Crimea and the Black and the Azov seas, with more than 1,000 drones used in some attacks in recent months.

Russia, meanwhile, has battered Ukrainian civilian areas with relentless strikes that seek to make normal daily life impossible and break public morale, especially through strikes on the power grid, as well as choking the economy.
The war has killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of Ukrainian civilians, Western analysts and officials say.
Six people were wounded in an attack on Russia's southern Krasnodar region, according to local authorities. The town is home to the Ilsky oil refinery, a frequent target of Ukrainian drone attacks.
Firefighters work at the site of a cardboard factory hit by a Russian jet drone attack Monday, in Odesa, Ukraine. (Nina Liashonok/Reuters)
In the Rostov region near the border with Ukraine, three people in the city of Azov, where two oil depots are located, were wounded by drones, Gov. Yuri Slyusar said.
Around 600 drones flew toward the Moscow region overnight, Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said. Most were downed far away, while 191 were shot down as they approached the Russian capital, he said.
Ukraine pushes back with long-range strikes
The strikes on Russia serve multiple purposes for Ukraine.

They have repeatedly targeted Russian oil refineries, which are an economic mainstay for Moscow. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed late Sunday that Ukrainian attacks have disabled more than 55 per cent of Russia's oil refining capacity.

Russian officials didn't comment on that claim, and independent verification wasn't possible. But in a rare acknowledgment of the strikes' economic impact, Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Oct. 1 that they had cost Russia roughly one per cent of its gross domestic product.

Ukrainian officials are keen, too, to make Russians feel the war at home, while mid-range strikes are disrupting Russia's front-line supply routes and hampering Moscow's efforts to get momentum on the battlefield, analysts say.

items: U.S. envoys talk to Zelenskyy in Dublin, after prior sitdown with Putin in Moscow
Russia-Ukraine talks mediated by U.S. end with news of 'good momentum,' large-scale prisoner swap

blocks.text: Kyiv says newly imposed speed limits on the U.S.-made Starshield system, SpaceX's military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service, have weakened Ukraine's air defenses. Ukrainian forces say they are adapting to that by launching pre-emptive attacks that hit Russian weapons production plants and sites that Russia uses to launch drone and missile attacks.
Kyiv also wants to show its supporters that it is still in the fight, as Moscow tries to depict its victory in Ukraine as inevitable and U.S.-mediated talks make no impact on the war.
There was no clear picture of the extent of damage caused by Ukrainian strikes in Russia. Moscow-based and local officials rarely provide details.
Zelenskyy calls Russian strikes 'brutal'
Ukrainians are bracing for what could be the hardest winter since the war began, as Russia repeatedly batters the power grid and denies civilians heat, light and running water.

Russian strikes on power lines and substations in the southern Zaporizhzhia and central Dnipropetrovsk regions left hundreds of thousands of people without electricity, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said Monday.
Zelenskyy says the Russian strategy is to bombard specific areas for days, flattening energy infrastructure.
Since the start of September, for example, the central Dnipro region has endured 131 strikes, while the Kyiv region around the capital has witnessed 125, he said.
Russian attacks violate Trump's 'energy ceasefire', says Zelenskyy
One person was killed and three were injured in a Monday morning strike on Dnipro, local officials said.
Just over the past week, Russia has launched more than 2,300 attack drones, 1,590 glide bombs and 15 missiles of various types against Ukraine, according to Zelenskyy.
They are "brutal strikes that are difficult to counter," he said on social media.

Four people were killed and three more injured in Russian shelling of towns and villages in the Donetsk region over the past day, said Vadym Filashkin, head of the Donetsk Regional Military Administration.

articles.title: ‘Orwellian’: HIV scientist’s ordeal lays bare Trump officials’ interference in grant-making
articles.summary:
Researchers forced to scrap original studies as NIH rethinks grants not in ‘alignment’ with administration’s priorities

Dr Jade Pagkas-Bather received her first grant from the National…

blocks.text: Dr Jade Pagkas-Bather received her first grant from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) in June 2025 – a milestone in any researcher’s career.

She planned to study basic income as a medical intervention: her randomized control trial would test whether monthly grants of $500-cash helped poor, HIV-positive young people in Chicago stick with treatment. Her hypothesis was as straightforward as it was cutting.

“Maybe taking care of your HIV isn’t your priority when you’re unhoused or hungry,” said Pagkas-Bather. That summer, she was through peer-review and about to be funded when NIH program officers started asking for changes, verbally and usually on a video call. “We had something that said we would include people of all gender identities in the grant. Program officers asked us to remove the term ‘gender identities.’ We had a clause that said Black and Latinx people experience more poverty than other people. They asked us to remove that.” There was also “concern” with the acronym for basic income grants (Big).
Pagkas-Bather removed it all, received funding and enrolled dozens of study participants. Then, in 2026, a bigger ask came: could she remove the entire idea of giving out cash?
She recounted being told: “You can’t use unconditional cash transfer and you need to remove any reference to this having an impact on policy.”

Pagkas-Bather’s experience is a glimpse into the Trump administration’s NIH renegotiation process, an opaque and “Orwellian” political review that uses a “text analysis tool” to flag grants not in “alignment” with the Trump administration’s priorities.

The process has injected uncertainty, confusion and woe into scientific grant-making at the NIH over the past two years. Renegotiations force program officers, who typically take pride in shepherding critical research, to flag grants on topics the Trump administration disfavors. Even as they do so, they must guess what the “no-no” words are: NIH director Jay Bhattacharya has repeatedly denied a list of banned words exists.

“Her story is not unique,” said Shalini Agarwal, special counsel at Project Democracy, who is representing Pagkas-Bather in a suit seeking class-action status, and alleging the government is violating the first amendment. “There are many other researchers in a similar situation who are being asked to subvert their own grant projects that have been peer-reviewed and approved for funding a year or more into the project.”
The number of scientists who have been through this process is unknown.

Data shared exclusively with the Guardian shows re-negotiations surged in the first two years of the Trump administration. In 2023, only 154 of more than 40,000 grants up for renewal changed their titles, abstracts or public health statements: 0.4% of all grants, according to an analysis by Grant Witness, an independent group that tracks canceled government grants.

Those changes increased 21-fold during the Trump administration. In 2025, 8.6% of all grants changed year-to-year, or more than 3,401 of the more than 39,000 grant continuations awarded by NIH. In 2026, 8.5% of all continuing grants changed, or 3,006 of the agency’s nearly 35,500 grants, according to an analysis by Grant Witness.

In the 2027 fiscal year, which just started, 64 grants have been renewed. Three have already seen changes. In one a study initially titled “The Black Zones”, which was to focus on African American neighborhoods, all mentions of “African Americans” was removed, and a new version referenced “Black Americans”. In another, an HIV grant that would study a specific viral subtype had text changed from including “men and women” to “a wide range of people”.

HIV grants are almost twice as likely to have been changed, data shows, and were especially hard-hit in early cancelations. In part, many likely undertook renegotiations because the Trump administration placed severe restrictions on scientific work in South Africa. In 2025, of the 1,795 HIV-related continuing grants, 305 were changed, or 17%. In 2026, 335 of 1,609 grant continuations were changed, or 20.8%.

“The censorship that’s happening now is, I think, pretty much unprecedented,” said Jeremy Berg, a former director of the National Institute of General Medical Sciences, who has closely tracked changes in grant-making at the NIH. “It’s very Orwellian in the sense that it’s purely double-speak,” he said. “It’s a way of exerting political control and control of the terms of the debate,” said Berg.
The Guardian asked the NIH how many grants have been changed, and about the “text analysis” tool employed by NIH.

The agency said “more than 5,000 new and continuation grants” have been re-negotiated, “to ensure the agency funds the most meritorious science, addresses urgent health needs, and sustains a robust biomedical research workforce”.

“During these grant renegotiations, grant scopes were substantively altered wherever possible to replace poorly defined, non-scientific or subjective concepts and variables with well-defined, scientific concepts that have objective and measurable variables,” an NIH spokesperson told the Guardian. “Renegotiation is a normal process that NIH has used for years on grants for various reasons. All renegotiated grants are assessed by human experts.”
after newsletter promotion

The NIH’s renegotiation process was set into motion in 2025, after court battles slowed down Trump administration grant cancellations. As the administration sought to change scientific studies, it developed a process of bringing grants into “alignment” with administration priorities – to name a couple, the belief that gender is binary and research into health equity is “unscientific”. Program officers who take pride in helping foster critical research are now tasked with renegotiating grants, often intuiting what might get flagged, said National Cancer Institute branch chief Sarah Kobrin.
“They are told to contact the investigators in case the investigators want to make changes,” Kobrin said. “We are compelled. We are not calling and saying, ‘Hey, could you change these words.’”
Instead, program officers must ask: “‘Hey, you know, if you want, you could change these words and it might work out well for you.’”
“It is certainly, certainly, certainly continuing,” she said.
Now, as a historic number of Democratic doctors and scientists prepare to take office, current and former leaders of NIH said Congress has years of work ahead to restore the agency.
Pagkas-Bather is one of 14 named plaintiffs in a first amendment lawsuit that argues such renegotiations and cancellations amount to censorship or, in legalese, “viewpoint-based discrimination”.

The Guardian has also covered other researchers involved in the lawsuit. In Pittsburgh, a group of researchers had funding cut for a study of Alzheimer’s disease risk in a low-income, majority Black neighborhood. The study was cancelled by the administration, leaving hundreds of aging residents without potential dementia diagnoses.

Ultimately, Pagkas-Bather was told that if she did not remove the cash payments from her $1.3m grant, she would need to find $1m in funding elsewhere. Seeing no path forward, she eliminated cash grants from her study and plans to use food and transportation vouchers as her intervention. She will need to ask each participant for consent again, since the study they signed up for bears little resemblance to the one she is now conducting.

“Not only would [Pagkas-Bather’s study] demonstrate that money empowers people to preserve their right to exist, but also thrive,” said Leslie McGorman, senior director of policy and strategy with AIDS United. “That is so threatening to this administration.”
A federal court hearing will determine whether the lawsuit filed by Pagkas-Bather and others will receive class-action status in November.

articles.title: ‘Visceral response’: flag campaigns inspire anti-racism organising across England
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Study shows people taking action against far-right intimidation such as 75-year-old taking to his bike at 2am to remove flags

Flag campaigns and far-right intimidation have…

blocks.text: Flag campaigns and far-right intimidation have sparked a wave of grassroots anti-racism organising across England in the past 12 months, according to research.

The Institute of Race Relations (IRR) says the widespread displays of St George’s cross and union jack flags have been accompanied by racist abuse and violence, with flags deliberately placed outside schools, mosques and care homes.
The report also warns that flag campaigns may be serving as recruitment grounds for far-right vigilantism, pointing to links between local groups and more militant anti-migrant networks.

But the report notes that the campaigns have also prompted ordinary residents to take action, from Quakers devising homemade tools to remove flags in Oxford to community groups documenting racist incidents in south-west London and establishing solidarity hubs in Nottingham.

blocks.caption: March against racism in Merton, London. Photograph: Merton against Racism

blocks.text: Sophia Siddiqui, the report’s author, said she had been struck by the anger and frustration among people who felt compelled to act. “One person I spoke to, a 75-year-old man who has never been an activist before, seeing what was happening around him really provoked a visceral response, where he just felt like he had to get on his bike at 2am and start taking down flags.”

Siddiqui said the campaigns had “backfired” in some communities. “Whenever flags had gone up, it had been met with community resistance, which had had the opposite effect of actually bringing people together.”
Last year, St George’s cross and union jack flags appeared across England in campaigns organisers described as patriotic, but which critics linked to racist intimidation and harassment.

Ryan Bridge, a co-founder of one of the initiatives, Raise the Colours, was charged earlier this year with 14 offences, including racially aggravated harassment and assault. Bridge pleaded not guilty to all charges earlier this month.
The report, Anti-fascism from below: resistance to far-right flag campaigns, draws on interviews with community organisers in Oxford, Birmingham, London, Nottingham and Worcestershire.

Siddiqui said flag campaigns had been accompanied by racist abuse against schoolchildren, Islamophobic harassment and racist graffiti, while flags deliberately placed outside schools, care homes and places of worship in multicultural areas had created “an atmosphere of intimidation”.

In Oxford, members of the Quaker community became so concerned about the displays that they devised their own method of removing them. George, a spokesperson for Oxford Quakers who didn’t wish to give his real name, said residents feared the flags were giving a false impression of a city with a long history of welcoming refugees and asylum seekers.
“What we really disliked was the colonising of our public space by people with opposing views to give the impression that Oxford was a xenophobic place, which it definitively is not,” he said.

With the council initially removing only flags considered hazardous, and council workers reportedly facing abuse and intimidation for attempting to take the flags down, the Quakers fashioned a tool using a blade attached to an 8-metre wooden pole to cut down flags.
“We just thought there must be another clever way that will be discreet and non-confrontational. That’s the Quaker way,” George said.

blocks.caption: A wall mural in Norwich. Photograph: supplied

blocks.text: In south-west London, Saqib Deshmukh, co-founder of Merton Against Racism, began documenting flag displays after spotting them on his regular running route in Colliers Wood. “I got on my bike to cycle around, and lo and behold, there were flags everywhere,” he said.
He set up a spreadsheet tracking flags and painted crosses across the borough, cross-referencing incidents with reports to the council. His group recorded nearly 50 incidents.
Deshmukh also described reports of racist abuse directed at Black and Asian residents in streets where flags had appeared, including near schools, nurseries and a care home employing migrant workers.
“This wasn’t done willy-nilly. This was very carefully orchestrated and thought through,” he said.
Despite residents lobbying councillors, contacting their MP and raising concerns at council meetings, Deshmukh said many flags remained until deteriorating weather brought them down.

In Nottingham, organisers have taken a different approach, establishing a solidarity centre in Hyson Green that offers food, legal advice, art workshops and a space for people from different backgrounds to meet.

blocks.caption: A member of the Worcester Patriots attaches union jack and St George’s cross bunting on to a streetlamp in Worcester, last year.  Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Jagdish Patel, who is involved in the initiative, said the aim was to tackle the economic insecurity and isolation that far-right groups exploit.
“We feed people, and by feeding people, people from all different backgrounds come together,” he said.

Elsewhere last year, counter-protesters vastly outnumbered the Worcester Patriots at a demonstration in Worcester, while Birmingham residents launched a citywide solidarity poster campaign. In Oxford, community pressure helped secure an injunction against unauthorised flags on lamp-posts, with Birmingham pursuing similar action.

But challenging far-right activity has carried risks. Patel described cases of white women being harassed for expressing sympathy towards asylum seekers, while the report documents activists facing threats, intimidation and online doxxing.
The IRR warns that flag campaigns may have provided a recruitment route into more militant far-right vigilantism.
Siddiqui pointed to the emergence of Patriotic Platform, which mobilised masked men at the ports of Kent and Portsmouth in September.
She said flagging campaigns, in seeking to impose their values on neighbourhoods and punish those who disagreed, “already had some of the hallmarks of vigilantism”.
Yet Siddiqui said the research had ultimately left her hopeful about the capacity of ordinary people to challenge the far right.

“What really stood out to me was the importance of building connections locally. It’s speaking to people, engaging with people, having those difficult conversations, and building those links at a local level,” she said.

articles.title: China says Xi, Trump, Putin to discuss 'world peace'
articles.summary: China says presidents Xi, Trump and Putin are going to have "in-depth discussions on global peace." Ukraine, Iran and denuclearization could also feature in the talks.

image.caption: Trump, Xi and Putin are set to hold their first-ever trilateral meetingImage: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Beijing said on Monday the leaders of the US, Russia and China will discuss "world peace" in their first trilateral summit in China this week.
Presidents Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin are due to meet in the southern Chinese city Shenzhen on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
China provided few details about the talks, but said they would involve "in-depth discussions on preserving global peace and promoting stability in relations."
"It will be of ground-breaking significance," foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told a news briefing on Monday, hours after Beijing confirmed the meeting.
Ukraine unlikely to be discussed
US President Donald Trump has previously said the meeting will be "interesting."
"We'll talk a lot of things, including denuclearization, but we'll be talking a lot of things. We're trying to end the war in Iran," he told reporters at a Florida airport on November 8.
Trump, Xi, Putin to hold first-ever trilateral meeting
In his brief remarks Trump avoided mentioning Russia's war in Ukraine.
According to a report published by the Wall Street Journal last month, Putin wanted the talks to broker a Ukraine peace agreement that would serve Moscow's interests.
US officials say Trump is not expected to raise the issue, AFP news agency reported.
Following his visit to China, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier told public broadcaster ARD that Xi appeared irritated when asked whether the trilateral talks would cover Ukraine.
"He explicitly pointed out that this is a European conflict, in which the Europeans must also be at the table," Steinmeier told ARD earlier this month.

blocks.caption: The past week, Russian attacks in Ukraine included more than 2,300 drones, 1,590 glide bombs and 15 missiles and cruise missiles, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saidImage: Nina Liashonok/REUTERS

blocks.text: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday asked Trump to not make any "surprises" on Ukraine with Putin during the talks.
"Please, no surprises. Continue to ‌play as part of 'Team Europe' and 'Team Ukraine'," he said.
Is an agreement on denuclearization possible?
Washington wants China included in future nuclear arms control deals, but Beijing insists the US and Russia must first reduce their arsenals.
China previously rejected Trump's proposal for broader disarmament talks following the expiration of a US-Russia nuclear treaty in February.

But according to the US State Department, in a call this week, top diplomats Wang Yi and Marco Rubio "agreed on the importance of meaningful leader-level conversations to advance goals such as peace and denuclearization."
AI and satellites: The new nuclear watchdogs?
United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said on Monday that if the three leaders "commit themselves to a meaningful denuclearization, it will be a great achievement for the world."
Where does the Iran war stand?
The Iran war, which began with US and Israeli strikes on February 28, is currently undergoing some de-escalation although major issues remain unresolved.
Both US and Israel are holding off major attacks as they held elections over the last weeks.

On the other hand, Tehran has continued seeking to control the Strait of Hormuz, a key transit point for global oil and natural gas supplies, while continuing to attack ships it considers unauthorized users of the waterway.
Iran's regime: Inside the system protecting its rulers
Before the midterm elections, US President Donald Trump said on October, "We may do another little Epic Fury," referring to US-Israeli strikes, without giving any timeframe.
Pakistan-mediated peace talks between the US and Iran on April failed to produce a durable settlement to the conflict.
As one of Iran's key economic partners, China has repeatedly sought to mediate in the conflict.
Beijing, says avoiding escalation is a "top priority."
It hosted leaders and diplomats from various Middle Eastern countries in recent weeks in an effort to persuade the parties to return to the negotiating table.

articles.title: Ukraine hits Kerch bridge between Russia and occupied Crimea
articles.summary:
Traffic temporarily restricted on key connection after bridge targeted during overnight drone barrage by Ukraine

Ukraine has hit the Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea with Russia, in a…

blocks.text: Ukraine has hit the Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea with Russia, in a symbolic blow that temporarily paralysed road traffic and left thousands of drivers stranded.

A Ukrainian kamikaze drone crashed into one of the bridge’s arches at 5.38am local time, local channels reported. Earlier drones could be heard buzzing above the structure, as Russian air defence units opened fire.
The extent of the damage was unclear. One report said the arch was listing at a 15-degree angle and “looked tired”.
The Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov, confirmed the “enemy” had launched an attack. “As a result, traffic will be restricted, likely until the afternoon,” he wrote on Telegram.
Russian officials said the crossing would remain closed while experts assessed its condition. About 2,000 vehicles were reportedly stuck in traffic jams on both sides.
In a call with reporters, the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, downplayed the incident. He said: “Minor damage is being assessed. ⁠Traffic across the bridge continues.”
Ukraine says the bridge is a legitimate target for its armed forces, and has made at least two previous attempts to blow it up.

In 2022 a truck laden with explosives damaged part of the road section. A second strike using a “sea baby” drone took place the following year. Russia has subsequently strengthened air defences and installed metal barges and boom barriers.

Overnight Ukraine launched 1,336 drones, in what the Kremlin says was one of the biggest attacks so far this year. About 600 were intercepted on their approach to Moscow, claimed the capital’s mayor, Sergei Sobyanin.

The barrage took place days before a summit in Shenzhen between China’s president, Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Putin. US officials say the talks will not focus on the war in Ukraine, where Russia’s military offensive has largely stalled.
after newsletter promotion

Ukraine says its retaliatory strikes are justified retribution for Russia’s own missile and drone barrages of its cities and energy grid – attacks that have killed hundreds of civilians and regularly knock out power and heating for millions. In recent weeks Russia has repeatedly hit two critical bridges in Kyiv over the Dnipro river.

Diplomatic efforts on ending the almost five-year war have so far gone nowhere. After a fresh round of talks in Abu Dhabi last week, Putin reiterated his hardline territorial demands and said any deployment of foreign troops would be seen in Moscow as a “continuation of war”.

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said on Friday the Trump administration had proposed that Kyiv gives Russia the eastern Donbas region – including towns and villages Russia does not control – in exchange for Nato membership or Nato-like guarantees.

Zelenskyy ruled out handing over territory. The details of possible US security guarantees were vague and did not feature American troops on the ground, he said, citing conversations with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and the real-estate developer Steve Witkoff. The emissaries last week saw Putin in Moscow.

articles.title: Ashes of exiled Nobel Laureate Miguel Ángel Asturias returned to Guatemala
articles.summary: The poet, writer and diplomat died in Europe in 1974 having been forced to leave his native country.

blocks.text: The remains of writer and diplomat Miguel Ángel Asturias have been buried in his native Guatemala 52 years after he died in exile.
His ashes were brought to Guatemala from Paris, where he had lived before his death from cancer in the Spanish capital, Madrid, in 1974.
Asturias was awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1967 for his vivid writings, which drew on the experiences of indigenous Guatemalans.
The urn containing his ashes was placed in soil gathered from different parts of Guatemala at a cultural centre named after him in Guatemala City.
His son, whose name is also Miguel Ángel Asturias, said at the ceremony on Sunday: "I can tell you, old man, that you are with us, you are in your homeland, you will sleep beneath your own skies."
Asturias, who was born in 1899, first moved to Paris in the 1920s to study ethnology.
Influenced by the surrealists, he wrote his first major work, Legends of Guatemala, a retelling of Maya origin legends and mythological tales, while in France.

Subsequent works, such as the 1946 novel The President and his Banana Trilogy, denounced the terrors of dictatorship in Latin America and the exploitation indigenous workers suffered on banana plantations.
Arguably his most famous novel was Men of Maize, published in 1949, which explores the struggles of indigenous communities as the world around them quickly changes and modernises.
Between 1944 and 1954, a period known as "Guatemala's 10 Years of Spring", he served in several diplomatic posts in Central and South America and continued writing.

But when the democratically elected Guatemalan President Jacobo Árbenz Guzmán was deposed in a CIA-backed coup in 1954, Asturias was stripped of his Guatemalan citizenship, his books were banned and he had to go into exile.
At Sunday's burial ceremony, Asturias's son said that the writer had "always wanted to be in Guatemala" but "political conditions did not allow him to".
The family only agreed to have the ashes moved from Père Lachaise cemetery in Paris to Guatemala after the current progressive president of Guatemala, Bernardo Arévalo, was elected in 2023.
Arévalo praised Asturias at the interment ceremony as "our voice in the world".

"He deserved to rest in the land he named and reinvented in his pages," said Arévalo, whose father Juan José appointed Asturias to the diplomatic service when the older Arévalo served as president during the 10 Year Spring.

The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) on Monday said it is monitoring online content that "seemingly" encourages violence amid ongoing protests as the country hosts the 2026 ASEAN Summit.

“We respect the public’s right to freedom of expression, peaceful assembly, and to seek redress from the government. But these freedoms should never be used as justification to incite violence or threaten public safety,” said CICC executive director Renato Paraiso in a statement.
The agency said it identified individuals whose online posts "seemingly promote or incite violence" in connection to the protests.
The CICC added that it is still assessing the credibility of the said posts.

"While the government recognizes the public’s right to air grievances and participate in peaceful protests, it will not tolerate attempts to incite violence or provoke unrest through online platforms," the agency added.

articles.title: Man sentenced over 'horrific' attempted murder of three children
articles.summary: Riad Bouchaker was sentenced after the attempted murder of three children in November 2023.

blocks.text: The attack took place outside Gaelscoil Choláiste Mhuire in Parnell Square, shortly after 13:40 local time on 23 November.

A group of 13 children, aged five and six, were lined up on Parnell Square waiting to go to their afterschool provision. Childcare worker Leanne Flynn was helping a little boy zip up his jacket when Bouchaker pulled his knife on the children.
A five-year-old girl was left with a lifelong brain injury after being stabbed in the heart.
Now eight, she is non-verbal and can only communicate by blinking, uses a wheelchair and has to be fed through a tube in her stomach as she cannot swallow safely by herself.
The judge said the child will never live independently and that her life, and the lives of her family, had been permanently altered.

He also noted that Flynn suffered life-threatening injuries, including a collapsed lung and the loss of a spleen, as well as profound psychological consequences and her services not being available to children.
The judge said she had acted fearlessly to protect the children and hoped she could return to work in the future, but said the possibility of such remains an unanswered question.
Judge Hunt said this was an unprecedented, highly unusual case involving a sudden, ferocious, sustained attack on young children and their childcare worker.
He said he had to mark the exceptional gravity of the offending against very young children and their carer, with a lethal weapon leading to consequences of the utmost gravity.
He said the circumstances were uniquely horrific and marked a profound assault on the most fundamental values protected by the criminal law.
The judge said the children happened to be selected because they were there and he was not yet sure what inference could be drawn from how Bouchaker found himself at their collection point.
At an earlier hearing, the court heard he received brain surgery in 2021 and a portion of his skull was removed, leaving a part of his brain vulnerable.
He suffered a head injury when members of the public intervened during the Parnell Square attack, after which he received hospital treatment for a month.

His defence team, which the judge ordered cannot be named due to safety concerns, said Bouchaker's cognitive function, memory, concentration, communication and decision-making were affected as a result of the impairment.
