blocks.text: November 16, 2026 | 3:56pm
Supreme Court Associate Justice Amy Lazaro-Javier speaks at an event as seen in a video posted August 2024.
SC video; Philstar.com screenshot

MANILA, Philippines — Supreme Court Associate Justice Amy Lazaro-Javier retired Monday, November 16, with the high court recognizing her for maintaining a zero-backlog docket throughout her judicial career.
Lazaro-Javier was conferred the Judicial Medal of Distinction, one of the Supreme Court's highest honors for judicial excellence, during a retirement ceremony held on October 27.
The award is given to retiring justices who leave no cases undecided beyond the 24-month period prescribed by the Constitution.

"Given to retiring members of the SC who leave no cases undecided beyond the Constitution's prescribed 24-month period, the medal recognizes distinguished judicial service that helps sustain the people's faith and confidence in the Judiciary," the Supreme Court said in a statement Monday.
The high court said Lazaro-Javier maintained a zero-backlog docket both at the Court of Appeals and the Supreme Court.
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. appointed former Commission on Audit chair Gamaliel Cordoba on November 13 to succeed Lazaro-Javier.
Cordoba is Marcos' third appointee to the Supreme Court, including the appointment of a new chief justice.

articles.title: AI in German classrooms: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'
articles.summary: The research points in one direction: If students aren't careful about how they use AI-enabled tools, then academic performance can plummet. It's a huge challenge for teachers.

image.caption: More than 90% of young Germans between the ages of 12 and 19 report using at least one AI applicationImage: Matthias Balk/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Jakob is 15 years old and attends a secondary school for more academic students, known in Germany as a gymnasium. He and his classmates have already been using artificial intelligence-enabled tools, or AI, for the last two and a half years.

"I had a French test today, and yesterday I had ChatGPT explain a lot of the topics to me again," the student told DW. Jakob isn't his real name, because he doesn't want to publicly admit he and many others of his age use AI to do their homework.
Math, German, English, chemistry and even physics: In one click, the solution or the path to a solution is available thanks to AI.
'Cognitive outsourcing'
In science, this is called "cognitive outsourcing." Basically, the required thinking is shifted to another device, whether that's a calculator, notepad or a large language model (LLM) like ChatGPT.

There's a difference with AI, though. A notepad or calculator can take over a step or two but rarely the whole thought process. That's not the same for an LLM, which can handle the entire problem-solving process.

Jakob admitted he's also had an AI help him with his homework. "But only when I was really stuck," he insisted. And he's also aware that it can become a problem when AI does all your homework. "The students who get good grades tend not to do that," he explained.

blocks.caption: Tablets are commonplace in many high schools and from there, it's just a short click to ask an AI for the answersImage: Hauke-Christian Dittrich/picture alliance

blocks.text: Franziska Müller has been a German teacher for several decades and is currently teaching senior classes at a gymnasium. Her name has also been changed for privacy reasons.
"They can't even think for themselves anymore," she told DW, complaining about some of her classes.

Even in ordinary classes, some of the students type their questions into their tablets or phones, asking for AI assistance. And should they be called upon in class, she knows that they're reading out the answers that the AI has prepared for them and hoping nobody notices.
Müller believes students these days are less able to comprehend text. "Because they read less and let AI summarize almost everything for them," she said.
Lower scores, thanks to AI
Several studies have reached very similar conclusions.

That includes the latest PISA (Program for International Student Assessment) study from September. PISA, which is run by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, regularly evaluates the abilities of 15-year-old students around the world.

"Students who report using AI chatbots get lower scores in science, on average, than those who don't use AI," Andreas Schleicher, the OECD director for education and skills, wrote in his report in October. "This includes using AI to summarize texts they had to read, conduct preliminary research on a new topic, or draft texts for writing assignments."

With participants from more than 90 countries, PISA is considered the largest international comparative study of 15-year-olds worldwide. This year, German 15-year-olds posted their lowest PISA scores in the 25-year history of the study.
Education in transition: How AI is changing teaching

"The connections are complex and depend heavily on how generative AI is used, but the central insight is simple: Just as we don't get fit by watching sports but by doing sports ourselves, learning doesn't come from consuming content, but from the mind's productive cognitive engagement with new material," Schleicher explained.
Put simply, those who don't exercise their brains risk becoming less intelligent.
How to deal with AI in class?
US think tank, the Brookings Institution, has already argued that the risks of using AI in education outweigh the benefits.

Its own research, which included young participants from around the world, speaks of students losing "fundamental cognitive and durable skills as they increasingly rely on AI to perform learning's intellectual work," as well as the decline of critical thinking, memory, perseverance and independent judgment.
But what can be done against the power of ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Gemini and Meta AI?
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani has banned the use of AI in public schools up to the eighth grade for the 2026 and 2027 school years — so that's up to about the age of 14 or 15.

Not everyone agrees this is the right thing to do. Julian Hinn, who teaches German to students aged between 15 and 18 in Germany, said class members can still use AI apps on their mobile phones. "And anyone who thinks they won't use it at home is ignoring reality," Hinn told DW.

blocks.caption: German teacher Julian Hinn said he uses AI strategically with older studentsImage: Julian Hinn

blocks.text: Germany's annual JIM study, which tracks teenagers' media use and device ownership, supports that view.

Ninety-one percent of young people surveyed in Germany, between the ages of 12 and 19, stated that they use at least one AI application. The study also reports that 74% use AI for homework and learning.
The last JIM study actually dates back to 2024 so those percentages might be even higher now. Data on AI use in Asia, Latin America and the US from the Brookings study show similarly high figures.

German politicians have recognized the problem. Although education in Germany is the responsibility of the individual federal states, the so-called Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, or KMK, has been issuing statements on the use of AI since 2024.
The KMK's statements have been rather vague though, saying only that students should be enabled to engage with AI in a critical, reflective and responsible manner.
Students should question AI, too
Teachers and students alike are aware that AI can be a powerful support in the classroom.
"The AIs simply explain things much better than textbooks," said Jakob, adding that he'll often get an AI to explain basic concepts to him.
Sometimes teachers can't respond like an AI, Hinn conceded. "The AI ​​can respond much better to the language and needs of the students."

That's why he thinks it's important to include AI in classes, starting from the 10th grade when students are around 15 or 16. Hinn doesn't think it should be introduced before that, when children's basic skills are still being developed.
In more senior classes, Hinn will encourage his students to question the AI critically. "We look at the quality of the solutions," he explained.

German teacher Müller has also integrated some use of AI into her lessons for older students. But in some aspects of the class, she also bans it altogether so that her students can focus on thinking for themselves.
"I understand very well that it's tempting to use AI," she said.

blocks.caption: Homework with AI? The temptation is great but teachers say students aren't doing themselves any favorsImage: Max Slovencik/APA/picturedesk.com/picture alliance

blocks.text: There are also other problems with AI in education. According to the Brookings study, students with basic skills can use AI to deepen their learning and progress faster.
But for children with gaps in their knowledge, they tend to adopt AI's errors, outsource their thinking and then fall even further behind. In this way, AI can exacerbate preexisting inequalities.
The PISA study notes that children from more affluent backgrounds often have a better start, and AI can widen that gap.

This is called the Matthew effect — the name comes from the biblical verse Matthew 25:29, "for unto everyone that hath shall be given." It basically means that early success in learning leads to better progress in the future, while early struggles equal a growing lag over time.
In the age of AI, teachers have become more motivated to challenge students to think independently and to consider their own personal autonomy.
Estonia adds AI to the classroom
Hinn, who also supervises the school newspaper, said: "I always tell everyone, you can use AI but the feeling of having written an article with your own pen is spectacular."

Both teachers also stress the idea of personal autonomy and responsibility. They believe this affects the students, especially because when they sit exams, they aren't allowed to use any aids or AI. And if they aren't able to solve their own problems, they will fail.
It's during exam time that the students really find out if they can solve those math, English or science problems by themselves.
Müller said one of her students recently confessed they were upset after a poor exam result. "He felt he simply couldn't think for himself anymore because of AI," she said.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: SC scraps bond rule for seafarers claiming disputed awards
articles.summary: The Supreme Court (SC) has declared unconstitutional and void the requirement for seafarers to post a bond before claiming disputed monetary awards and damages pending appeal or judicial review.

blocks.text: Published November 16, 2026 3:38pm
The Supreme Court (SC) has declared unconstitutional and void the requirement for seafarers to post a bond before claiming disputed monetary awards and damages pending appeal or judicial review.

In a press release issued Monday, the SC En Banc partially granted five consolidated petitions filed by seafarers, labor groups and maritime schools questioning provisions of Republic Act No. 12021, or the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers, as well as its implementing rules and related issuances.

Under Section 59 of the law, monetary awards for wages, statutory benefits and undisputed amounts were immediately executory. However, seafarers were required to post a bond before claiming disputed amounts and damages to guarantee repayment if the ruling was later overturned or modified.

The SC ruled that the bond requirement violated the constitutional guarantees of due process and equal protection by imposing a financial burden on seafarers seeking to enforce favorable labor judgments, a requirement not similarly imposed on other workers.

“The Court held that the bond requirement violated the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses of the Constitution. It imposed a financial burden on seafarers seeking to enforce favorable labor judgments and subjected them to a disadvantage not similarly imposed on other workers,” the SC said.

“While recognizing the State’s interest in preventing ambulance chasing and protecting the maritime industry against unrestituted awards, the Court found that these objectives did not justify the challenged restriction on the execution of monetary awards,” it added.
Section 59 also allowed the Department of Migrant Workers’ Agarang Kalinga at Saklolo Para sa mga OFW na Nangangailangan (AKSYON) Fund to cover the bond premiums.

The SC likewise declared this provision unconstitutional, saying the use of public funds to pay private bond premiums violated Section 29(1), Article VI of the Constitution, which requires public money to be spent strictly for a public purpose.
The High Court also struck down provisions of Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) Department Order No. 247, Series of 2025, that enforced the bond requirement.
The SC emphasized, however, that the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers remains valid and enforceable, except for the provisions expressly declared unconstitutional or void.
“The law therefore remains valid and enforceable, except for the provisions expressly declared unconstitutional or void,” it said.
Associate Justice Maria Filomena Singh penned the decision. — MCG, GMA News
Follow GMA News Online on Facebook for real-time news and developments in the Philippines and around the world.

articles.title: Mozambique's justice under scrutiny as Venancio Mondlane faces trial
articles.summary: The trial of opposition politician Venancio Mondlane begins in Mozambique on Tuesday. The former presidential candidate is facing five charges, including incitement to terrorism.

image.caption: After parliamentary and presidential elections in November 2024, supporters of opposition politician Venancio Mondlane took to the streetsImage: ALFREDO ZUNIGA/AFP

blocks.text: The trial of Venancio Mondlane will shape the political future of Mozambique, and influence how much trust citizens place in state institutions.

From November 17, the country will be watching the opposition politician and former presidential candidate as he faces five counts, including publicly advocating crimes and inciting collective disobedience and terrorism after the October 2024 elections.
If convicted, he could be sentenced to more than 20 years in jail.
'Nothing to do with violence'
Mondlane has denied all the charges, and said he never called for violence. In fact, he said, his public statements were meant to prevent violence.

"I have more than enough evidence that numerous statements I made went in exactly the opposite direction," he told DW during a Septembervisit to the European Parliament in Strasbourg. "I have more than sufficient evidence that numerous statements I made were in exactly the opposite direction."
'Nothing can prove that I am the one who promoted violence'

The post-election protests had two main goals: To pressure authorities to investigate extrajudicial killings of members of Mondlane's political movement, and to find out the truth about election results.
"These were the fundamental issues of our entire protest," he said. "This has absolutely nothing to do with violence."
Where does criminal incitement begin?

In the October 2024 presidential and parliamentary elections, Mondlane ran as a presidential candidate with the support of the left-wing opposition party Podemos. Afterwards, he did not recognize the official election results.

blocks.caption: Demonstrations in Mozambique continued for weeks after the October 2024 electionsImage: Jaime Álvaro/DW

blocks.text: The election saw Daniel Chapo of the Frelimo party declared winner. Frelimo has governed Mozambique since independence in 1975.

After the elections were called, Mondlane and his supporters protested. For months, there were demonstrations, strikes and road blockades as well as violent clashes with security forces nationwide. According to reports from civil society groups, more than 400 people died. Shops and public facilities were looted or destroyed.

The public prosecutor's office has alleged a connection between Mondlane's public calls to action and the violence. The indictment is based on his live broadcasts on social media, in which he called for protests, strikes and civil disobedience.
Albino Forquilha, who heads Podemos and is Mondlane's former political ally, is expected to testify at the trial. However, he told DW that he would not appear as a witness for the prosecution.

Forquilha said he would report his own observations of the protests and would only testify to what he personally experienced. He cannot predict whether his statements will benefit Mondlane or the state.
Prosecution overstating some aspects, says critic
Baltazar Fael, a prominent Mozambican lawyer, argues that the prosecution's case is problematic.

Speaking with DW, he warned against equating indictment with conviction. "What we currently have is an indictment by the public prosecutor," he argued. "And this does not mean that the accused has already been convicted."
The court will hear arguments from both sides and must decide whether what happened constitutes a criminal offense. Predicting the outcome is difficult.

blocks.caption: Lawyer Baltazar Fael says he has doubts about the trialImage: Silaide Mutemba/DW

blocks.text: Fael is particularly critical about the charge of incitement to terrorism. For this charge to be valid, a plausible connection between Mondlane's statements and specific acts must be proven. Acts of violence that occurred following his calls to action will not be enough to convict him on this charge, Fael said.

The question is whether Mondlane actually intended to incite terrorist acts. "What power did Venancio Mondlane actually have to incite people to commit all these crimes?" Fael asked, adding that, after reading the indictment, he believes the prosecution is overstating some aspects of its case.
Is the case politically motivated?
There are also questions as to whether the trial might be politically motivated in some way. For years, Mozambique's justice system has been criticized because of potential political interference.
Fael said several factors have raised doubts. "The timing of the trial and the circumstances that led to it — namely, a challenge to the election results — are clearly political in nature," he said.
Additionally, the speed at which the trial was prepared might also give the impression that there's some political pressure at work here, he added.
What an opposition leader's trial means for Mozambique

Adelino Muchanga, chief justice of Mozambique, has emphasized that his court will decide the case based on facts. But observers are still asking how independent the judiciary can be when the defendant is one of the most prominent critics of Mozambique's political leadership.

The Supreme Court's decision not to allow a live broadcast of the trial has drawn further criticism. Mondlane's defense requested a live broadcast but was denied by the court, which reasoned that such a broadcast could endanger the safety of those involved, influence or intimidate witnesses and disrupt proper conduct of the trial.

Critics see this refusal as a setback for transparency, especially since another recent, prominent trial, the so-called "hidden debt scandal" where state-owned companies secretly borrowed billions from international banks, got extensive media coverage.
Social unrest remains
Additionally, the causes of the protests that sparked this trial have not disappeared. DW's interviews with citizens in the northern Mozambican city of Nampula make this clear.
"The people still want the same thing," one resident told DW. "They wanted Venancio to become president."
Another Nampula resident pointed out that "the population protested against hunger and the lack of jobs for young people. And that's legitimate."

Still, some in Nampula just want to see closure, preferring to have peace and an end to the demonstrations. Even if the economic situation could be better, the country has to return to normality at some stage, they argued.
Additional reporting by Amos Fernando and Conceicao Matende in Maputo.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: PNP ready to assist in Quiboloy's possible extradition to US
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Monday said it is ready to assist in the possible extradition of Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KOJC) leader Pastor Apollo Quiboloy to the United States should a…

blocks.text: Published November 16, 2026 3:30pm

The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Monday said it is ready to assist in the possible extradition of Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KOJC) leader Pastor Apollo Quiboloy to the United States should a court issue an order for police assistance.

“We will only follow lawful orders from competent courts. If they will include us at meron po silang kautusan na ibigay sa atin,” PNP spokesperson Police Brigadier General Allen Rae Co said at a press briefing.
(We will only follow lawful orders from competent courts. If they will include us and they have an order to give us.)
“Whether it's to assist in the transfer and to secure the person of pastor sa pagpunta po sa airport or otherwise very much ready po ang inyong PNP to assist and to render assistance,” he added.
(Whether it's to assist in the transfer and to secure the person of pastor when going to the airport or otherwise your PNP is very much ready to assist and to render assistance," he added.
On November 12, the Makati Regional Trial Court issued an extradition arrest warrant and hold-departure order for Quiboloy and two of his co-accused, the Department of Justice (DOJ) earlier said.

On behalf of the US government, the DOJ filed an extradition petition on Monday against Quiboloy, Teresita Tolibas Dandan, and Helen Panilag in connection with their charges of international human trafficking, sex trafficking, conspiracy, and bulk cash smuggling.
Quiboloy’s lawyer, Israelito Torreon, said on Nov.13 that his client was not surprised by the extradition petition filed against him and is prepared to face the proceedings in court.

Torreon clarified that he does not represent Quiboloy in the extradition proceedings, noting that his duties are limited to the religious leader's pending criminal cases before the Pasig and Quezon City courts.
He confirmed that Quiboloy has already been notified of the extradition petition, which the Department of Justice (DOJ) filed on Monday on behalf of the United States government.
“Please be informed that Pastor Apollo C. Quiboloy has been informed of the extradition proceedings filed against him,” Torreon said.
“They do not come as a surprise to him. He has expected them, and he is ready to face them in court, through the proper legal process and before the proper forum,” he added. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: US basketball player arrested with 34kg of cannabis at Nigerian airport
articles.summary: The anti-drugs agency says the American attempted to leave the airport, abandoning his luggage with the drugs.

blocks.text: A professional American basketball player has been arrested in Nigeria with 33.95kg (75lbs) of cannabis in his luggage at the main airport in Lagos.
The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) identified the player as Greene Da'monte Khiree, 28, from the US state of Georgia, who it said had arrived from Thailand via the United Arab Emirates.

According to the agency, the suspect said he had been playing professional basketball in Thailand and was visiting to Nigeria to "build networks" for his career. He has not publicly commented on the allegations.
The agency said an examination of the suspect's phone had pointed "to his knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity".
In statement on Sunday, the agency he was arrested on Wednesday after airport officials noticed him abandoning his two checked-in bags and attempting to leave with his carry-on bag.
The two bags, which bore his name, contained 32 packs of the drug known as "Loud", a potent strain of cannabis, the agency said.
A tracking device was also recovered from the bags, the agency added.
The International Basketball Federation (FIBA) lists a player by the name Damonte Greene, with the most recent appearance at the Phuket Elite Cup in Thailand, on 26 September.
Nigeria, once regarded primarily as a transit hub for drug trafficking, has increasingly become a producer, consumer, and distributor of illegal drugs, according to the UN.

Recent NDLEA operations have uncovered several industrial-scale methamphetamine laboratories, raising concerns about links between Nigerian drug producers and Mexican cartels seeking to manufacture and export the drug.
In September, the agency said it had dismantled a meth lab and arrested a Mexican suspected drug kingpin who was allegedly attempting to flee Nigeria through Lagos.
Methamphetamine, commonly known as meth, is a highly addictive synthetic drug that can cause severe psychosis, heart attacks or stroke.

In August, a social media influencer suspected of links to an international drug trafficking network was arrested after the authorities seized cocaine worth nearly $28m (£21m), which was destined for the UK.

articles.title: Marcos calls for renewed political will, cooperation to achieve SDGs
articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Monday called for a renewed political will, stronger partnerships, and evidence-based cooperation to realize the United Nations Sustainable Development…

blocks.text: Published November 16, 2026 3:07pm

President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Monday called for a renewed political will, stronger partnerships, and evidence-based cooperation to realize the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (UN SDGs) by 2030.
During the 16th ASEAN-UN Summit, Marcos pointed out that only 36% of the accessible SDG targets “are on track” less than four years away from the 2030 deadline.

“Achieving these goals requires renewed political will, stronger partnerships with the private sector, and cooperation that is evidence-based and responsive to the needs of its members, especially developing countries,” the President said.

Marcos said that through the ASEAN-UN Complementarities Initiative, ASEAN is hoped to substantially contribute to advancing progress in these goals by aligning ASEAN 2045 with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.
He likewise welcomed the UN General Assembly’s adoption of the resolution commemorating the 50th anniversary of the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia.
Marcos said that the adoption served as a “reaffirmation of conduct for interstate relations in our region and beyond.”
He also noted the first year of the ASEAN-UN Plan of Action 2026-2030.
“Our cooperation spans peace and security---from combating trafficking in persons, online scams, and illicit drugs, to peacekeeping and keeping Southeast Asia free of nuclear weapons,” Marcos said.

“It extends to trade facilitation, digital transformation, the blue economy, the ASEAN Power Grid, and sustainable minerals development. It also covers health, food, security, disaster management, climate action, and the protection of women, children, persons with disabilities, and science and technology cooperation,” he added.
BARMM polls

Secretary-General António Guterres, on the other hand, congratulated the Philippines for what he described as a “successful conduct” of the first parliamentary polls in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).
He said the elections fully consolidated a “remarkable peace process” in the region.
“This should serve as an example well beyond the Philippines and this region,” Guterres said.
UN concerns
The UN chief, however, lamented the impacts of the tensions between Russia and Ukraine, as well as those in the Middle East, Strait of Hormuz, and the Red Sea, on ASEAN.
“I want to reaffirm the unconditional commitment of the United Nations to defend the rights and freedoms of navigation in all situations,” Guterres said.
He also expressed concern over the continuing crisis in Myanmar.

“Human suffering has reached epic proportions. I call on all parties to protect civilians, uphold international law, and allow safe, sustained, and unhindered humanitarian access,” he said. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: ‘It’s like the 16th-century version of doomscrolling’: the Book of Miracles may fetch £1m at auction
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Public institutions get first chance to bid for rare ‘wonderbook’ of apocalyptic visions and extreme weather

In one illustration, five suns blaze down on Leipzig in 1551. In…

blocks.text: In one illustration, five suns blaze down on Leipzig in 1551. In another, blood rain falls on Rome in 1456. In a third scene, dated 1552, monstrous hailstones batter the Dutch city of Dordrecht during a storm so fierce people feared Judgment Day had come.

Created during the mid-16th century, when earthquakes, storms, floods and other extreme weather events were often interpreted as ominous warnings from God, the Book of Miracles contains 167 paintings of apocalyptic visions, celestial wonders and meteorological phenomena.
It is the only known copy. To this day, no one is sure why it was created.

blocks.caption: A scene from the Book of Miracles: blood rain falls on Rome in 1456. Photograph: Christie’s

blocks.text: Now, public institutions will have their first chance to bid for the Book of Miracles since scholars learned it existed. It is expected to fetch between £700,000 and £1m when it is auctioned in London on 10 December, as the star lot of the Christie’s valuable books and manuscripts sale.
Members of the public will also have a rare opportunity to see it in person for six days before it goes under the hammer.

For nearly half a millennium, scholars were unaware of its existence. Found in the library of a small baroque castle in southern Germany nearly 20 years ago, the manuscript, which from 1550s Augsburg, was put up for auction alongside the castle’s furniture, carpets and tankards in 2008 and sold for just over £100,000.
Shortly after the sale, the manuscript entered the private collection of Mickey Cartin, one of Connecticut’s biggest contemporary art collectors.

blocks.caption: A scene from the Book of Miracles: a plague of locusts in Poland, 1527. Photograph: Christie’s

blocks.text: Eugenio Donadoni, Christie’s international specialist in medieval and Renaissance manuscripts, said the book was an “exceptionally rare” German wonderbook.

“German wonderbooks functioned as the sensationalist mass media of their day,” he said. “They were used by Lutheran theologians such as Martin Luther and Philip Melanchthon to further their Protestant eschatology, but crucially – with all the depictions of comets, cosmological events, natural disasters, all verified by witnesses, with exact dates and geographic coordinates – they laid early foundations for empirical observation and reporting. They mark a shift from medieval to Enlightenment.”
He expects the sale will attract collectors of both historic and modern art because some of the scenes, which are painted in watercolour and gouache, are “super surrealist … almost Dalí-esque”.
“If it weren’t for the little captions, which are obviously 16th-century German, some of them look so vividly modern … it’s really jaw-dropping,” Donadoni said.
The scenes depicted include a plague of locusts arriving in Poland on a “terrible wind” in 1527 and the North Sea flooding the coast of Frisia – in what is now the Netherlands and Germany – in 1230.
Other pictures are of fiery comets and eclipses, while scholars think an illustration of “wondrous dragons” flying across the sky over Bavaria in 1533 depicts the northern lights.

blocks.caption: A scene from the Book of Miracles: ‘wondrous dragons’ cross the Bavarian sky, 1533. Photograph: Christie’s

blocks.text: Underneath each scene, a German picture caption describes what is happening and where and when the event took place.
after newsletter promotion

“All of these events are portentous,” said Donadoni. “The artists of the Book of Miracles, relying on contemporary broadsheets, chronicles and histories, have condensed into pictorial form the concerns of an age that was gripped by an anxiety – and learned curiosity – about the future.”

The book records how uneasy people felt about climatic anomalies at a time of doctrinal disunity, when there was growing interest in documenting and cataloguing visible, tangible scientific phenomena, he said.
“It’s really fascinating … it is a window into how Europeans were dealing with the impending end of the world, political uncertainty and extreme – and strange – weather events.”

The five suns over Leipzig, for example, is thought to depict the optical illusion of a parhelion, more commonly known as a sun dog. “You see in the sky various different rings of light and it looks like suns,” Donadoni said.

blocks.caption: A scene from the Book of Miracles: five suns  over Leipzig in 1551. Photograph: Christie’s

blocks.text: “Blood rain” occurs when high concentrations of red-coloured dust particles, usually from the Sahara, mix with water droplets in rain clouds. “Many of these things have actual rational scientific explanations to them,” Donadoni said.

He said he imagined that leafing through the pages of the book in the 1550s was similar to bingeing on bad news on social media today: “I think it could be a little like the 16th-century version of doomscrolling.”
In this way, the book straddles a momentous turning point in history. “We’re right at that period where the superstition of the middle ages turns into the age of scientific discovery,” Donadoni said.

Till-Holger Borchert, the director of the Suermondt Ludwig Museum in Aachen, has studied the manuscript and said the first time he saw it, his reaction was: “Wow”. “It’s one of a kind,” he said. “It grabs you by your heart or your soul or your belly.”
He said he thought £1m was a “very conservative estimate” of its value. “It [the final price] could possibly be much more,” he said.

A facsimile of the manuscript was published in 2013 that got people “really excited” about it, Borchert added, and since then the Book of Miracles has become “a kind of icon for people who are interested in apocalyptic things”. It would be wrong to value it merely as an historical document: “It’s more than that. It speaks to us, to our generation.”

articles.title: Andy Burnham to say Brexit ‘has not worked’ and he will sign new deal with EU
articles.summary:
Prime minister is to meet European leaders at summit this week and secure agreements that ‘could raise GDP by 0.4%’

Andy Burnham will say on Monday that Brexit “has not worked” and that he…

blocks.text: Andy Burnham will say on Monday that Brexit “has not worked” and that he will sign a new deal with the EU.

It is the latest in a string of comments by the prime minister criticising Brexit, after he told the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday that the UK has “lost more than we gained” through leaving the EU.

Burnham is due to meet European leaders at a summit this week and secure agreements that he says could raise GDP by 0.4% – about £17bn – including on food and farming, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme.

Speaking at the lord mayor’s banquet in the City of London, Burnham is expected to argue that Boris Johnson’s promise to take back control was not delivered, and that the country was left with a needlessly hard Brexit that created barriers for businesses and damaged its economic potential.

“It’s like the Emperor’s New Clothes – where no one is prepared to say the obvious truth. Well, I say it as I see it. And to be frank, the emperor has nothing on,” Burnham will say. “The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained.”
Burnham is to say he will sign an agreement with the EU, so long as it:

items: Is consistent with the Labour manifesto and the government’s red lines.
It improves the Brexit deal and brings it closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016.
And it passes the so-called “Makerfield test” by delivering real, tangible improvements in people’s everyday lives.

blocks.text: “This is a win-win,” Burnham is expected to say. “It illustrates our new approach. Not adversarial. No longer burning bridges – but being constructive and positive, showing that we can come together to confront shared challenges.”
However, the EU relations minister, Hamish Falconer, told the BBC on Sunday that the UK could have a “voice in the room” under a new deal with the bloc, but no vote on EU food policies.

He added there could well be an “exit clause” in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment, explaining that the EU was “worried” about the possibility of a future Reform or Conservative government undoing the agreement.
after newsletter promotion
The BBC understands the clause is a result of EU concerns about the possible cost of having to rebuild facilities for border food safety checks which were put in place after Brexit.
Meanwhile, Johnson, the former Conservative prime minister who resigned over Partygate in 2022, has said Britain would “absolutely” vote for Brexit again if Burnham forced another vote on the issue.
He told the Telegraph: “It is madness to escalate the Brexit issue as your political priority.
“He will impale himself and his party on this point, and he needs to move off it because he won’t win – because the reality is that people are not fools.”

articles.title: Monday briefing: The many stages of the UK-EU relationship – and what’s next
articles.summary:
In today’s newsletter: From situationship to a possible makeup, a look at the evolving relationship, and the bloc’s big feelings about the future

Good morning. Ahead of the hotly anticipated…

blocks.text: Good morning. Ahead of the hotly anticipated UK-EU summit this Friday, Andy Burnham is expected to make the reset of our relationship with Europe the pivotal theme of his white-tie speech at the lord mayor’s banquet in London tonight.

The prospect of closer ties – and the possibility of going “all the way” to reversing Brexit – has been met with jubilation and relief in some quarters and vehement opposition in others, while around Westminster and across the media the psychodrama has been spiralling for weeks.

At this point, I’m reminded of that Robert Burns couplet: “O wad some Pow’r the giftie gie us / To see oursels as ithers see us!” What does the EU think about all this? Are they ready to reverse what leading figures have repeatedly described as a colossal act of self-harm? Or are they viewing this latest iteration with bombastic side-eye? I posed these questions to Jennifer Rankin, the Guardian’s Brussels correspondent. First the headlines.
Weekend roundup

items: UK news | A woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 has waived her right to anonymity to campaign for a staggered age of consent, which would make it illegal for adults over a certain age to have sex with 16- and 17-year-olds.

Youth unemployment | Andy Burnham has pledged to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment before a watershed review, promising “a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood in the modern world”.

Environment | The strongest El Niño in centuries has added urgency to UN climate talks in Turkey as vulnerable countries face “compounding” crises. In other Cop31 news, queer and gay protesters defied a crackdown on LGBTQ+ rights in Turkey to lead a civil society climate march.

UK news | Two people aged 22 and 23 have died after their car was hit by a BMW being pursued by police. West Yorkshire police said four people had been arrested and appealed for witnesses to come forward.

Air transport | The Trump administration says Friday’s four-hour nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that delayed or cancelled thousands of flight stemmed from routine maintenance. The US transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, blamed prior presidents and Congress for the stoppage.

blocks.text: In depth: ‘This is a real priority for the EU, in almost emotional terms’

blocks.caption: While official discussions about the UK rejoining the EU are not on the agenda this week, there is genuine enthusiasm about the matter. Photograph: Andy Rain/EPA

blocks.text: Ahead of the summit, the pro-Brexit polity has been in broadcast mode: headlines from the past few days include: “Burnham’s plot to rejoin the EU would leave the average UK household £6,500 poorer” (Express); “Taxpayers funding pro-EU university courses” (Sunday Telegraph); “Staggering cost of PM’s EU reset” (Daily Mail).

Stay Out, a new campaign against rejoining the European Union, launched last week. While the guy you really want to hear from right now – David Cameron, the prime minister who lost the 2016 Brexit referendum – has insisted the UK’s problems have nothing to do with its exit from the EU.
Even within the Labour fold, there are rumblings of unease from MPs and unions.

But the one-day summit in Brussels this Friday does not include any formal discussion of rejoining: instead, the EU and UK hope to sign deals on food and drink, emissions trading and the youth experience scheme (a work and study exchange programme).

Still, the mood music is upbeat. Back in September, when Burnham first opened the door to a Brexit reversal, French president Emmanual Macron responded: “welcome back.” while Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez said: “Spain would welcome Britain’s return with open arms.”

The enthusiasm is genuine, says Jennifer. Indeed, some European diplomats have told her the technicalities could be wrapped up within a year because the UK remains closely aligned with the bloc in so many areas. “It would be such a vote of confidence in the European project for a country to decide to return after voting to leave”.
Situationship: what’s at stake at this week’s summit?

Though Burnham has predicted “some long nights” of negotiation this week, Jennifer says there’s optimism on each side as the first two deals on food and drink and emissions trading were largely agreed.

There are two sticking points with the youth exchange deal. First, the Home Office wants to limit numbers to the UK to keep migration figures low. Second, there’s disagreement over whether those students would pay UK domestic rates of tuition fees or the international rate, which is four or five times higher for some courses.

The UK is offering concessions on tuition fees if it can join Made in Europe, the EU legislation designed to protect domestic manufacturing from cheap Chinese competition. But the EU says it can’t make a deal on Made in Europe this week, because the law is still at a draft stage.

And here’s where it gets complicated. The European Commission has proposed delaying an agreement on tuition fees for six months, which could allow time to get the UK into Made in Europe, a diplomatic win for Britain. But there’s pushback from member states who want to pin down the UK on tuition fees this week. “This is a real priority for the EU, in almost emotional terms,” Jennifer says. “Lots of EU officials and diplomats studied in the UK, or their children did, and they felt this was one of the big losses of Brexit, that these person-to-person links were being eroded.”
On-again, off-again: what else could get in the way of closer working?

In play at Friday’s summit will also be a future deal on Britain’s return to the EU’s internal electricity market and a joint migration pact, with the UK pushing for access to EU crime databases to tackle the small boats crisis.

Member states are already working hard to smooth things out on the electricity front, to stop it becoming a sticking point. A couple of weeks ago, Jennifer reported on leaders from Germany, Denmark and elsewhere calling for deeper cooperation on clean energy – which she reads as an attempt to head off a row about how much the UK should contribute to EU cohesion funds for the evident privilege of cutting red tape, easing trade and, ultimately, reducing costs.
A similar row over UK contributions scuppered negotiations last year on our entry into a €150bn EU defence fund.

It could also be a challenge for the UK to realign with the EU on farming, after changing to a payment model that puts more emphasis on delivering environmental benefits. And past UK governments have been lukewarm about EU AI regulation, devised post Brexit.
Conscious partnership: will the EU welcome future closeness this week?

I learned long ago there’s no such thing as a stupid question, so I ask mine now: will there be a moment on Friday when Ursula von der Leyen offers the equivalent of Macron’s “welcome back”? Will there be a “just give us six months to sort out the paperwork Andy” vibe?

The European Commission president is, by nature, a cautious politician, Jennifer tells me, so she doesn’t expect anything so specific. “I’m sure she – and António Costa, the European Council president – will get asked about it at the press conference, and they’ll want to send a signal about the UK being welcome to rejoin.”

But behind closed doors, in Brussels and other capitals, what Jennifer hears repeatedly is that it’s up to the UK to decide what it wants. And, while the prospect of Brexiteer Nigel Farage in Downing Street has faded in recent months, there remains a deal of caution about the vicissitudes of UK politics. “Now the Burnham government is exploring the options, but there’s also an awareness that you could have a very different government in a few years’ time,” she says.
It’s not you, it’s me: what else is Europe worrying about?

The EU and its member states are preoccupied with far weightier problems: the war in Ukraine (Volodymyr Zelenskyy attends every EU summit), the rise in support for the far right, street protests, hybrid threats from Russia, a trade deficit with China that has reached a staggering €1bn a day in 2026.
“There are so many other issues crowding on the agenda,” says Jennifer. So it’s not all about us? “That’s actually been the theme of my decade of reporting from Brussels,” she says with a laugh.

There’s profound concern about the prospect of Marine Le Pen winning the French presidential elections next year, which could tip the bloc into a crisis if she pursues her resolutely anti-EU agenda, which includes reducing France’s substantial contribution to the EU budget.

Beyond that, there’s a broader question about increasingly divided and unstable politics across member states. “Every single member state has to agree to the UK’s re-entry,” Jennifer reminds me. “Who knows what the EU will look like in 2030 when Britain could be having a rejoin referendum?”
after newsletter promotion
The week to come

items: Tuesday | The work and pensions secretary Alan Milburn’s long-awaited review into why increasing numbers of young people are falling out of work and education, is expected to be released.

Thursday | German chancellor Friedrich Merz, French president Emmanuel Macron and UK prime minister Andy Burnham will be among around 20 heads of state meeting in Berlin to discuss defence funding for Ukraine, and to establish a unified position on future peace negotiations in its war with Russia.
Friday | This marks last day of the world’s biggest annual climate conference, Cop31, in Turkey, with final negotiations taking place.

The front pages

Hidde Burgmans, from the Netherlands, looks for ancient trees – and he’s created an app of the same name to help people find remarkable old trees around the world, from Malaysian baobabs to the Fortingall yew in Perthshire, Scotland, thought to be an astounding 5,000 years old.

Users can review remarkable old trees around the world, and upload their favourites to the Ancient Trees app. “On Tuesday somebody photographed a tree in Edinburgh. Today, someone in Freiburg,” said Burgmans. “That just makes me happy. I thought it was quite a niche, geeky thing, but apparently more people are interested in ancient trees than I thought.”

articles.title: Philippines, ASEAN leaders back faster rollout of power, fuel solutions
articles.summary: ASEAN leaders are accelerating regional fuel-sharing and electricity-grid agreements as Middle East conflict disrupts supplies.

blocks.text: November 16, 2026 | 1:42pm
People use their phones in front in the press centre during the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila on November 15, 2026.
AFP / Nhac Nguyen

MANILA, Philippines — Southeast Asian leaders moved to accelerate regional fuel-sharing and electricity-grid agreements as conflict in the Middle East continues to disrupt energy supplies and drive up costs.
ASEAN member states backed the full implementation of the ASEAN Petroleum Security Agreement during meetings Sunday, November 15, Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro said.

The agreement was originally established to allow member states to share crude oil and petroleum products during supply disruptions. It was expanded to cover liquefied natural gas at the 43rd ASEAN Ministers on Energy Meeting in October 2025.
Lazaro said the petroleum agreement would complement other regional energy-security initiatives, including the ASEAN Power Grid.
The ASEAN Power Grid seeks to link national electricity systems through cross-border infrastructure by 2040, allowing countries to trade power and draw on supplies elsewhere in the region.
ASEAN members signed an enhanced memorandum of understanding on the initiative Sunday.
Energy Secretary Sharon Garin reaffirmed the Philippines' commitment to expanding regional electricity trade and attracting investment in cross-border infrastructure.

"As ASEAN Chair in 2026, the Philippines looks forward to working with fellow Member States and partners to advance cross-border electricity trade, attract investment and deliver a stronger ASEAN Power Grid for our communities and economies," Garin said.

The Philippines also signed a two-year cooperation agreement with the Economic Research Institute for ASEAN and East Asia, aligning its work with the Philippine Energy Plan and the Asia Zero Emission Community initiative.
Under the partnership, the Department of Energy will draw on the institute's regional research to develop strategies addressing the country's growing electricity needs.

Pressure on Philippine energy. The Philippines remains under a State of National Energy Emergency declared in March, when conflict in the Middle East intensified supply pressure around key shipping routes, including the Strait of Hormuz.
Volatile fuel prices have since added to inflationary pressure at home. Headline inflation reached a three-year high of 7.8% in October, driven in part by higher energy and transport costs.

The Super El Niño could place further strain on electricity supplies. The DOE has warned that the weather pattern, expected to persist into mid-2027, could push the Luzon, Visayas and Mindanao grids into red-alert conditions.

articles.title: Mexican drug lord Felix Gallardo dies at 80
articles.summary: Felix Gallardo was considered to be the architect of Mexico's modern drug-trafficking trade. He died of multiple organ failure at the age of 80.

image.caption: In 2011, Gallardo's family had complained that he was being mistreated in prisonImage: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo — known as the "godfather" of Mexico's modern drug trade and a notorious trafficker himself — died in a hospital on Sunday. He was 80.

"After remaining under observation with a guarded prognosis, he died on November 15 at the medical facility" after "he suffered multiple organ failure," said a statement from the security ministry of the state of Jalisco, where he was being held.
An inmate's death

Having founded the Guadalajara cartel, one of Mexico's first major drug syndicate which would later birth the Sinaloa cartel, Gallardo had been imprisoned since 1989 and was transferred to a private hospital two days ago.

He was arrested and sentenced to 40 years in prison on drug-trafficking and weapons charges tied to the cartel. While already behind bars, he faced a seperate prosecution for the kidnapping and murder of a US drug-enforcement agent. This earned him an addition 37-year prison sentence and his reputation as Mexico's most notorious trafficker.
Felix Gallardo had been an inmate in a maximum-security prison in western Jalisco state even after his lawyers repeatedly sought house arrest on the grounds of his deteriorating health.
We met a cartel killer — who really runs Mexico?
The life of Felix Gallardo
Gallardo was born in 1946 in the Northwestern state of Sinaloa, which would later become synonymous with narco-trafficking.
He initially worked as a police officer and bodyguard for a local governer but soon transformed into a power criminal, known as the "boss of bosses."

Gallardo, along with others, set up the Guadalajara cartel becoming the first to move cocaine to the US on a massive scale. He was also the first to forge an alliance with Colombian drug cartels including Pablo Escobar's Medellin cartel.
In the 1970s, Gallardo rose to prominance as his narcotics empire expanded on the back of bribed law enforcers and the use of light aircrafts to move drugs across the continent.
His rise and fall as a Mexican drug lord was ortrayed on screen by Mexican actor Diego Luna in the 2018 Netflix hit series 'Narcos: Mexico.'
In his final years, Gallardo suffered poor health and was blind in one eye, practically deaf and unable to walk on his own. He maintained that he was innocent.

articles.title: Canada could work with Chinese automakers if US trade talks fail, says Carney
articles.summary:
Ahead of Apec summit, PM says ‘Canada is going to move forward either way’ when asked if Chinese investment was leverage in US negotiations

The prime minister of Canada, Mark Carney, said…

blocks.text: The prime minister of Canada, Mark Carney, said the country could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with the US president, Donald Trump, failed to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.

Carney’s comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.

“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of US trade actions.”

He said on Monday that negotiations with the US remained his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers. A day earlier in Manila, in the Philippines, Carney said any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry.
Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in US negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction.
“If they [Canada’s auto workers] are not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”

The Detroit Three – Ford, General Motors and Stellantis – operate factories across Canada, the US and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the US from Canada.

Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would need proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including Canadian critical minerals used in electric vehicles.
“It’s not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.”

Under a January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.
Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada’s auto industry and create jobs.

The deal drew criticism from Ontario premier Doug Ford, whose province is the center of Canada’s auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the US market.

Trump’s tariffs have disrupted Canada’s auto industry, which relies heavily on cross-border production. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the automaker shifted planned Jeep Compass production from Brampton, Ontario, to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant.
Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior US officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained.

articles.title: Rocket from Boeing-Lockheed firm fails mid-flight, destroys payload of Amazon satellites
articles.summary: A Vulcan rocket suffered an anomaly about 10 minutes after liftoff from Florida, failing to deliver 40 Amazon Leo satellites to orbit. It was the first total mission failure in the company's history.

image.caption: The mission and all 40 satellites were lost after the rocket suffered an anomaly about 10 minutes into flight, according to ULAImage: Manuel Mazzanti/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: A Vulcan rocket operated by United Launch Alliance, a joint venture of Boeing and Lockheed Martin, failed about 10 minutes after liftoff from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Sunday. The incident resulted in the loss of all 40 AmazonLeo internet satellites aboard, marking the company's first mission failure.

"Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit," ULA said in a ​statement.
The exact cause was not immediately clear.
"Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us something. Since the anomaly just occurred, we don't have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today," ULA added.
The failed launch marks ‌a major setback for ULA's new flagship rocket. The two-decade-old ⁠company was set to begin a regular cadence of launches for Amazon's burgeoning satellite internet program.

blocks.caption: The Vulcan rocket was launched from the Cape Canaveral launch site in FloridaImage: Manuel Mazzanti/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Mission failure raises fresh concerns over US launch capacity
The failure is expected to trigger a lengthy technical investigation, potentially grounding the Vulcan rocket for months.

US companies could face reduced launch capacity amid other rocket failures, industry challenges and uncertainty over the future availability of SpaceX's Falcon 9, the world's most active rocket. SpaceX is no longer accepting bookings for the rocket.

"There is risk with any launch, and that's especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01," Amazon said in a statement, referring to Sunday's mission. "ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they'll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan."
Is ULA in trouble?

ULA was formed in 2006 through the merger of Boeing's Delta rocket program and Lockheed Martin's Atlas rocket program. The incident marked the first total mission failure in the company's history, ending its record of successful mission deliveries since its formation.

Sunday's launch was Vulcan's fifth since its debut in 2024 and its first in nine months. The gap followed separate technical investigations into its solid rocket boosters and core BE-4 engines, which are supplied by Blue Origin, the space company founded by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos.

The solid rocket boosters had come under scrutiny after anomalies on Vulcan's previous two flights, including a February 2026 mission for the US Space Force. Both missions successfully delivered their payloads into orbit despite the booster problems.
US national security clearance for Vulcan under scrutiny

The Space Force paused Vulcan's national security launches pending the outcome of an investigation and the implementation of corrective measures. Sunday's Amazon mission was expected to provide further data before the military decided whether to clear the rocket for those launches.

An investigation traced the problem to the engine's main oxygen valve. Blue Origin subsequently developed modifications for the BE-4 engines supplied to ULA, and the engines installed on Vulcan were retrofitted, ULA officials said.
It remains unclear whether the BE-4 engines played any role in Sunday's failure.
Nearly 400 satellites launched as Amazon challenges Starlink
Amazon relies on third-party launch providers to deploy satellites for its Leo internet network. Other launch providers have also faced technical problems and delays.
Blue Origin's New Glenn explosion in May occurred during a ground test, just days before the rocket was scheduled to launch Amazon Leo satellites.
Repeated launch setbacks have complicated Amazon's efforts to compete with SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet network, which has more than 11,000 satellites and millions of customers worldwide.

blocks.caption: Amazon previously used ULA's Atlas V rockets for its launches (File Photo)Image: Joe Marino/UPI Photo/IMAGO

blocks.text: SpaceX's advantage over satellite internet rivals is partly due to its ability to use its own rockets to deploy satellites. Other companies rely on external launch providers, adding to the cost and complexity of building their constellations.

Before Sunday's failed mission, Amazon had launched 398 Leo satellites across 14 missions since 2025, according to Reuters. That represented about 12% of the 3,236 satellites the company needs for global coverage. Amazon had hoped to begin initial internet services this year.

articles.title: 3 friends complete 8,000-km canoe journey across Canada, arriving in Vancouver
articles.summary: After more than 200 days, thousands of kilometres and countless hours on the water, three longtime friends from Toronto completed their cross-Canada canoe journey on Sunday at Vancouver's Jericho…

image.caption: From front to back, Will Vyse, Georges Kirijian, and Nolan Aziz arrive at Jericho Beach in Vancouver on Sunday. (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: British Columbia·New

After more than 200 days, thousands of kilometres and countless hours on the water, three longtime friends from Toronto completed their cross-Canada canoe journey on Sunday at Vancouver's Jericho Beach.
Trio spent 219 days travelling through 6 provinces to raise money for northern, remote Indigenous communities

Nolan Aziz, Will Vyse and Georges Kirijian, all 24, received a warm welcome from family, friends and supporters who gathered near the Jericho Sailing Centre to celebrate the end of their 8,000-kilometre expedition.
The crowd cheered as the trio stepped ashore, with some supporters breaking into a rendition of O Canada.
The three men set out from Tadoussac, Que., in April as part of their canoe expedition, travelling through six provinces along rivers and lakes, often far from major cities.

items: Paddling across Canada one waterway at a time.

blocks.text: “I wanted to take the more unconventional route because I am very deeply fascinated with being the first to do something or trying something new…it’s deeply enthralling in a way,” Vyes told CBC News.
"There's a lot of magic in all the tiny hidden creeks and rivers that are out of the way that no one goes to.”
The trio believe they have completed the longest single-season canoe expedition ever recorded at more than 200 days.
From left to right, Nolan Aziz, Georges Kirijian, and Will Vys stand together while spectators sing O Canada during their arrival to Jericho beach in Vancouver. (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press)

They previously finished a 60-day trip in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic, and decided to see if they could push that further and travel across the country in support of Truth North Aid, a charity that helps northern and remote Indigenous communities.
Their goal is to raise $1 million for the charity, and so far have raised just over $130,000.
Journey with plenty of challenges
The expedition was not without difficulties.
The trio paddled long distances each day, camped outdoors almost every night and sometimes had to carry their canoe over land when waterways became impassable.
Vyse said cold weather in Quebec delayed their progress, forcing them to carry their canoe for weeks while waiting for frozen lakes to thaw.
"We had to portage for like three weeks straight because the lakes just weren't thawing," he said.
The red canoe used by the three friends to complete their journey rests on Vancouver's Jericho Beach. (CBC)
Some portages stretched between 50 and 80 kilometres.
In B.C., the group faced a lengthy detour to avoid the dangerous currents of Hells Gate on the Fraser River.
They also encountered stormy weather and a bear near one of their campsites.
Kirijian said travelling in a single canoe meant they had to make careful decisions about safety.

items: Cross-Canada canoe journey raising funds for remote northern and Indigenous communities

blocks.text: "We're one canoe, we're three guys. We can't have any redundancy when it comes to any kinds of accidents in the water," he said. “We're always just going into things knowing we just have one boat, we cannot [be] rescued.”
But the journey also offered memorable experiences and some powerful insights, said Vyes.
“I think people are a lot better than we realize. Strangers are just friends we haven’t made yet,” he added.
Connections along the way
Among those welcoming the trio to Vancouver was Peatr Thomas, who travelled from Manitoba for their final landing.
Thomas met the paddlers when they stopped in his community during the 150-year-commemoration of the Bloodvein River First Nation's treaty signing.
He said the group showed an interest in learning about Indigenous communities and their relationship with the land and water.
The trio of canoeists were greeted by family with hugs and tears following their final landing. (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press)
"They also just wanted to know the perspective of the Indigenous peoples and the history and how we sort of connect with the land and the water as well," Thomas said.
Aziz said travelling across the country helped him appreciate the connections between Canadians from different regions and backgrounds.
“What we really saw, despite all the microcosms of different cultures that we have in this country ... we all have this shared national identity as Canadians and it's really beautiful,” he said.
With files from Ali Pitargue and The Canadian Press

articles.title: Yemeni forces' retreat leaves Houthis in control of key Red Sea waterway
articles.summary: Saudi-backed forces say they are moving troops from the Bab al-Mandab Strait to defend the interim capital Aden.

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Pro-government forces said troops were being moved to defend the interim capital, Aden (file photo)

Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia have said they are withdrawing from an area overlooking the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, leaving it under the control of the Iran-backed Houthi movement.
Yemen's military said it was redeploying troops from the key shipping gateway at the southern end of the Red Sea to defend its interim capital, Aden.

The shift ends a weeks-long offensive to try to secure the area near the waterway after the Houthis seized it in a surprise offensive in September, squeezing global oil exports and prompting thousands to flee.
Houthi-run media reported later on Sunday the group had taken control of the territory. Saudi Arabia has not commented.

Pro-government forces said they had "secured" the strait in early October as they sought to retake crucial ground from the Houthis, who said they had captured areas including Perim Island at the mouth of the strait and the strategic port city of Mokha a month prior.
Watch: Why is the Bab al-Mandab Strait so important?

But the Saudi-backed forces fighting on behalf of Yemen's internationally recognised government said on Sunday they were withdrawing to reinforce troops elsewhere, with the southern city of Aden a "priority".
The Reuters news agency reported a Southern Armed Forces statement which said troops were being withdrawn "from Dhubab Airport and the Bab al-Mandab area".
It said the decision had been made with the aim of "strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats".
The Houthis said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway when they captured it, but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.

However, the seizure contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia responded with hundreds of air strikes, while the Houthis launched hundreds of drones and missiles at its cities and infrastructure.
The UN has estimated that nearly 330,000 people have been displaced in Yemen as the fighting has since escalated. Hundreds of people are reported to have been killed.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from its capital Sanaa.
The conflict escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

articles.title: Australian MP who lost both legs in alleged car attack discharged from hospital
articles.summary: The MP was allegedly run down by a car outside her electorate office four weeks ago.

blocks.text: Australian politician Helen Haines, who lost both of her legs after police say she was deliberately run down with a car, has been discharged from hospital.
The independent MP was struck outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, on October 19, in an alleged attack which horrified Australia.

Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official. He is yet to enter pleas.
Haines, 65, has been discharged, the Alfred Hospital said on Monday, after four weeks and several surgeries which resulted in the amputation of her legs.

Haines, known for supporting stronger climate action and helping establish a national anti-corruption commission, entered parliament in 2019 as the Member for Indi after working as a nurse and midwife.
Victoria Police has said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police, remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.
Nugent's father said he and his wife had been long-time friends of Haines, and Nugent's lawyer has said his client has mental health concerns.
The incident sparked a reckoning in the country more broadly over the tone of public debate.
Though a motive is still unclear, politicians, law enforcement, and experts have said heated public discourse is heightening the threat of political violence in the country.
