articles.title: Yemen: Anti-Houthi forces pull back as rebels advance
articles.summary: Forces aligned with the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia are seeking to strengthen control over the interim capital Aden as the Iran-backed Houthis approach.

image.caption: The fighting in Yemen has been going on for years, with Saudi Arabia and Iran supporting opposing sidesImage: Mohammed Al-Wafi/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Southern Armed Forces group allied with Yemen's UN-recognized government and backed by Saudi Arabia said Sunday they had repositioned themselves away from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Why are troops moving away from Bab el-Mandeb?

The Southern Armed Forces said the repositioning is intended to secure the southern city of Aden, "and the neighboring governorates, as well as strengthening the frontlines and addressing existing threats."
Aden, which has a population of over a million people, is the interim seat of the Yemeni government, formally known as the Presidential Leadership Council (PLC).
The Southern Armed Forces also intend to end the Houthi siege over the strategic southwestern city of Taiz.
Nearly two million people live in Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city.
The siege is raising fears of famine for residents, as well as a possible medical crisis as hospitals face restricted supplies.
Can Yemen's government turn the tide against the Houthis?
Houthis advancing towards Aden
The Houthis control much of northwest Yemen, including the capital Sanaa.
The rebels are a Shiite militant group backed by Iran. The US, Canada and several other countries regard them as a terror organization.
The Houthis in September launched a rapid offensive against the PLC, seizing much of the coastline along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean.
It is also a key corridor for maritime trade and energy shipments.
The Houthis have taken control of the major port town of Mocha in September, firming their grip over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The latest redeployment of the Southern Armed Forces is likely to give the rebels even more control over the strategic area.
Sources told AFP news agency that Houthi forces are now just 60 kilometers (less than 40 miles) from Aden.
The conflict between the Yemeni government and the Houthis has lasted for over 10 years.
The fighting in Yemen, the poorest country in the Arab world, has been fueled by the wider rivalry between Iran and Saudi Arabia.
More fighting between Yemen's Houthis, Saudi Arabia

In recent weeks, the Houthis have been launching frequent attacks on Saudi Arabia. On Sunday, the rebels claimed that they targeted the King Khalid International Airport and financial district of the Saudi capital, Riyadh. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed the alleged Houthi attack.

articles.title: Teenager Andreeva caps stunning week with WTA Finals title
articles.summary: French Open champion Mirra Andreeva caps her stellar season with a hard-fought victory over Elina Svitolina to win the WTA Finals.

blocks.text: For Mirra Andreeva, the thought of her first WTA Finals singles campaign was so stressful that it gave her "a little breakdown" in a practice session before the tournament.
The 19-year-old may have been nervous on arrival at Indian Wells, but she leaves California as the champion, having been the standout player of the week.
The French Open winner produced a hard-fought 7-5 6-3 victory over Elina Svitolina in Sunday's final to become the youngest champion of the event in 22 years.
The Russian has now risen to second in the world rankings - and she will start the 2027 season just 293 points behind top-ranked Elena Rybakina.
Andreeva did not drop a set on her way to the title and lost only 26 games across her five matches.
She raised her arms in celebration after beating Svitolina before racing to celebrate with her team, which includes 1994 Wimbledon champion Conchita Martinez.
"I am super thankful to my team for pushing me to my limits, for forcing me to do stuff when I don't want to do anything," Andreeva said.
"Thanks for fighting with me, thanks for forcing me to do everything that I have to do and not asking any questions!"
As well as £2.55m in prize money, Andreeva also won a custom purple Mercedes - and joked she was happy to remain a "passenger princess" until she passed her test.
One of the most notable parts of Andreeva's performance has been her increased maturity.
In March, she swore at the Indian Wells crowd after suffering an early defeat in the venue's WTA Tour tournament, and she has struggled to control her emotions, external on court in the past.
However, she showed little sign of that during this tournament.

Against Svitolina, one of the grittiest players on the women's tour, she lost a break lead three times across the two sets. Each time, she reset admirably, upping her aggression on her backhand in particular to put pressure back on her opponent.
After losing serve in a mammoth nine-minute game in the second set, Andreeva marched back to her chair and then broke Svitolina from 40-0 down in the next game to stay in front.
While her serve was not at its best, Andreeva still saved nine of the 12 break points she faced and hit 19 winners to Svitolina's 10.
"This fighting mindset helped me to get more brave and aggressive in the important moments," Andreeva told Sky Sports.
"This is just a dream. I had a little breakdown in my practice just before Indian Wells because I was so stressed.
"I didn't want to lose a match in the group. It's amazing."
Andreeva had only won one of her six matches against top-10 players in 2026 coming into the tournament.
She has beaten three top-10 players en route to the title, including a demolition of four-time major champion Aryna Sabalenka on Wednesday.
She also laughed off an incident before the tournament where private comments Jessica Pegula made to her coach about Andreeva - including calling her a "diva" - were live-streamed.
Just as she did when she won the French Open, Andreeva ended her speech by thanking herself - a twist on a quote she "stole" from rapper Snoop Dogg.
"I want to thank myself for always doing the hard work and for never quitting," she said.
"For not taking the days off, for working every day and committing to what I have to do - just thanks to myself."

articles.title: Goodbye, overtourism? Sustainable travel gains ground
articles.summary: As tourism booms across Latin America, alternative forms of travel are gaining ground. Making your holiday more sustainable means rethinking who calls the shots, who invests and who benefits.

image.caption: Punta Cana, Dominican Republic — a tourism hot spot in Latin AmericaImage: Erika Santelices/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Latin America is currently one of the world's most dynamic tourism regions. According to UN Tourism, the United Nations agency responsible for promoting responsible tourism, international arrivals in South America grew by 7% last year, while Central America saw a 5% increase, both above the global average.

But the boom comes at a price: overtourism. In some destinations, the sheer number of visitors is creating environmental and social problems, fueling tensions and raising questions about who really benefits from the business.

One famous example is Machu Picchu, the Inca citadel in Peru, which lures up to 5,600 visitors a day. In 2025, Peru's official watchdog warned that more tickets were being sold than permitted, potentially putting the site at risk of being added to UNESCO's List of World Heritage in Danger. The UNESCO World Heritage Committee has already expressed its concern.

blocks.caption: People are flocking to Machu Picchu, the Inca citadel in PeruImage: Michalakis Ppalis/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: In a bid to protect the Galapagos Islands and its bountiful ecosystems that inspired Charles Darwin, Ecuador doubled the entrance fee for foreign visitors to $200 in 2024. Even so, pressure is mounting to construct new hotels and tourist apartments. And in Mexico City, the influx of tourists and digital nomads into neighborhoods such as Roma and Condesa has fueled protests over rising rents.

blocks.caption: The Galapagos Islands introduced an entrance fee for foreign visitors to $200 in 2024Image: Alie Skowronski/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What can be done to make tourism more inclusive and sustainable? That's one of the industry's biggest questions. At ITB Americas, an international travel trade fair in Guadalajara, Mexico, DW spoke with three experts.
Sustainable travel moving from niche to mainstream

Richard Bazan is a regional manager for the Americas at Planeterra, a nonprofit organization that promotes and supports community-based tourism. He said several trends are emerging: group sizes are shrinking and travelers are seeking more intimate experiences.
"Where groups of 20 used to travel together, now it's four or five," he told DW.

So-called "nature-positive" tourism is also gaining traction, with travel programs that help fund, for example, reforestation projects. Bazan said even all-inclusive resorts are realizing that they can no longer shut themselves off from their surroundings. Instead, they need to offer authentic experiences that connect visitors with the destination.
"Community-based tourism is no longer a niche," he said.

blocks.caption: Mexico has been trying to contain a record surge of foul-smelling sargassum seaweed, fueled by a mix of nutrient-rich runoff and shifting ocean conditionsImage: Alfredo Estrella/AFP

blocks.text: Pressure for change is also coming from travelers themselves. According to Booking.com's 2025 annual survey, which polled 32,000 people in 34 countries, 93% said they wanted to make more sustainable travel choices. For the first time, more than half (53%) were aware of tourism's impact on local communities, not just the environment.
Communities know what's best for their land

Sarah Payne, director of the Reset Tourism Fund at the UnTours Foundation, pointed to the underlying problem. In the traditional tourism business model, most of the money generated never reaches local communities, the people who actually live with the influx of visitors.

"Access to financing is key, yet extremely difficult for communities," she explained. The financial products on the market tend to be expensive and inflexible, as tourism is considered a high-risk sector. Her foundation's fund offers low-interest loans with flexible repayment terms. Its guiding principle is that communities generally know what's best for their own land.

Sebastian Munoz, co-founder of Rutopia, a platform specializing in ecotourism and community-based tourism, has brought his experience from the nonprofit sector into social enterprise. His believes tours must be designed in partnership with communities so they feel a sense of ownership, rather than seeing them as something imposed from outside.
Saving Ladakh: Locals lead sustainable tourism drive

Bazan, meanwhile, thinks community-based tourism should not be approached as a humanitarian project, but through a market-driven lens: understanding what visitors are looking for and then planning hand-in-hand with the local community. In other words, building bridges between these two distinct worlds.
"It's not sustainable to create a product if no one comes to experience it," he said.
The challenge: Rethinking growth

The big question is how to grow without sacrificing sustainability. For Bazan, that decision doesn't belong to the tourism industry. Communities themselves must decide how they want to grow, and outside players should not pressure them. Their role, he said, is to amplify local voices, not to bring solutions or investments. "We have to learn to listen," he said.

The impact of community-based tourism is difficult to measure, Munoz acknowledged, because it has social impacts that go beyond the numbers. He cited the example of the Indigenous Mixtec community in Mexico that receives tourists interested in learning the local language. Suddenly, children who today speak only Spanish began joining the classes and asking their grandparents to teach them the language, too.

For Munoz, community-based tourism can be a powerful tool for valuing cultural and regional diversity. It's about creating value over the long term — and that, he said, is where the real experience for visitors lies.
The experts agree that change is slow. But they argue it's worth the effort: If there is more respect for local people and environments, in the end, everyone goes home happier.
This article was originally written in Spanish.

articles.title: Zelenskyy urges removal of Starshield limits on Ukraine
articles.summary: Ukraine's government says the throttling of satellite-based internet system prevents Kyiv from intercepting Russian attacks.

image.caption: Zaporizhzhia was targeted overnight by russiaImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the US should remove any restrictions on the Starshield satellite internet system being removed.
Kyiv is "counting" on the move due to severe damage to civilian infrastructure as a result of Russian attacks, Zelenskyy said, also adding photos from eight locations in his country.
"The protection of lives and Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this," Zelenskyy posted on his X account.
The sattellite-based internet system was limited to slower speeds in October, with the limitations only being lifted due to Ukraine's criticism.

Ukraine leader Zelenskyy said he had instructed several ministries, including the Ministry of Defense and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, to "work as closely as possible" with the US and Starshield owner Elon Musk's SpaceX, also saying the system's throttling helped Russian attacks.

blocks.caption: A building was heavily damaged due to a Russian drone in Chornomorsk.Image: Nina Liashonok/REUTERS

blocks.text: According to Zelenskyy, Ukraine's interceptor drones are not effective due to losing connection with operators at the speed of 161 kilometers per hour. This results in the drones not being able to hit Russian drones or rockets.
Russian attacks continue

The past week, Russian attacks in Ukraine included more than 2,300 drones, 1,590 glide bombs and 15 missiles and cruise missiles, Zelenskyy said, calling Moscow's strikes "brutal" and saying they are "difficult to counter."
The US government and SpaceX gave in part contradictory answers to the question of who was responsible for the Starshield speed limit.
A Russian strike on the port city of Chornomorsk resulted in six injuries and damaged energy infrastructure, local authorities said.

blocks.caption: Zaporizhzhia was attacked several times in the past daysImage: Iwan Fedorow/Ratsverteidigung des Gebiets Saporischschja

blocks.text: According to the authorities, a facility operated by DTEK Odesa Electric Networks was hit, thus leaving some 41,000 customers without power on a temporary basis.
Six people were also injured after Russian attacks on the city of Zaporizhzhia, with one of those injured being a two-year-old boy, according to Ukraine's emergency services.
Estonia said Russia was responsible for an attempted arson attack on a drone factory, with the border between the two countries to close, citing "clear evidence" Moscow is behind the attack.
Secret schools keep Ukrainian kids learning under occupation

articles.title: Czechia: Thousands protest against public media reform
articles.summary: Hundreds of thousands of people gathered to protest against the government's plan to abolish broadcasting fees. Critics say the nationalist coalition would like to secure control over the media.

image.caption: Protesters traveled from around Czechia to attend the protestImage: David W Cerny/REUTERS

blocks.text: A protest against plans to abolish broadcasting fees in Czechiadrew between 350,000 and 450,000 people in Prague, organizers said.
The amount of protesters resulted in overcrowded public transport, with many people traveling from other cities by bus and train.
According to protesters, the plan could bring public broadcasters under the control of the country's right-wing government under billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis.

The government would like public broadcasters to be financed by the state budget rather than through fees, arguing that while the plan will not affect editorial independence, broadcasters need to cut costs.
Critics accused the Czech government of wanting to secure more influence through the decision.
The suggested media reform would result in public media's budget being cut down by 15 percent.
Government denies takeover attempt
Babis himself defended the plan last week, saying that his government is not interested in controlling or nationalizing public media.
"None of what the people are protesting against… is true," Babi said.
Foreign Minister Petr Macinka also replied to the criticism by accusing the protest's organizers of turning demonstrations into a business model.
Since its introduction in April, the plan resulted in several large-scale protests, with Czech TV and radio going on a one-day strike in protest against it.

blocks.caption: Hundreds of thousands of people attended the demonstration in PragueImage: David W Cerny/REUTERS

blocks.text: International groups have criticized the plan, including the European Broadcasting Union, the European Federation of Journalists and Reporters Without Borders.
International criticism
The current coalition in Czechia is made of Babis's ANO party, the far-right SPD and the Eurosceptic Motorists.

blocks.caption: Prime Minister Andrej Babis rejected the protesters' criticismImage: Michaela Rihova/CTK Photo/IMAGO

blocks.text: While the protests also saw the current coalition being criticized, polls show ANO still enjoys some 30% of support.
Per the Reuters Institute Digital News Report for 2026, trust in the media in Czechia is low and stands between 30% and 33%, with public broadcasters still being considered "the most trusted brands."

articles.title: Estonia closes border to Russia after suspected drone factory arson
articles.summary: Estonia has accused Russia of conducting hybrid warfare after a drone factory was set alight in Viimsi. Now it will close its border crossings at the start of December.

image.caption: Estonia was one of the few EU states that allowed border crossings to and from RussiaImage: Hendrik Osula/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Estonia foiled an attempted Russian arson attack on a drone fractory, authorities said on Sunday, prompting the country to close all border crossings with its larger neighbor.
Prime Minister Karsten Michal said that Russia's GRU intelligence service had attempted to sabotage the Estonian defence company Threod Systems in Viimsi on Saturday night.
He said "extensive damage" had been averted after a response by law enforcement, who detained the suspected attackers.
"This is part of Russia's broader hybrid war against Europe, with the aim of decreasing support to Ukraine and pressure on Russia," Michal said.
There was no immediate comment from Russia.
Estonia to close border crossings with Russia
Hours after the announcement, Estonia's Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said the country would close all border crossings with Russia by December 1.
"Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences. Attempts to intimidate, destabilise, or undermine our security will not go unanswered," he said on social media.
"Closing the border crossings will reduce Russia's ability to conduct hostile activities in Estonia and strengthen our efforts to prevent sanctions circumvention."
How Baltic states are responding to Russia's hybrid warfare
Tsahkna said he informed his Finnish, Latvian, and Lithuanian counterparts of the decision.
Estonia has a number of border crossings with Russia, and has until now remained one of the few European Union member states that allowed crossings.

articles.title: Nearly 1,600 migrants arrive on Spain's Canary Islands in one day
articles.summary: The majority of the migrants who arrived on the islands on Saturday came from Senegal, Gambia, and Guinea. The surge in arrivals to the Canaries comes after Spain's Ceuta recently faced a migration…

image.caption: Most boats departing for the Canary Islands come from Mauritania (FILE: November 12, 2026)Image: Borja Suarez/REUTERS

blocks.text: Nearly 1,600 migrants arrived on the Spain's Canary Islands in one day, Spanish news agency EFE reported Sunday, using tallies from the Spanish government's Maritime Safety and Rescue Society.
What do we know so far about the migrant arrivals on the Canaries?
Most of the 1,580 migrants who came ashore on Saturday landed on the island of El Hierro. They arrived aboard 15 wooden fishing boats.

Most of the migrants came from West African countries such as Senegal, Gambia, and Guinea. Between Friday and Saturday, over 2,300 migrants in total arrived on the islands, according to the Spanish authorities.
The Canary Islands, whose shortest gap with Africa is around 100 kilometers (around 62 miles), faces a migration crisis.

Spanish Territorial Policy Minister Angel Victor Torres Perez visited the town of La Restinga on Sunday, which lies on the southernmost tip of El Hierro. She met with residents of the town and thanked them for "their solidarity and commitment" as the island witnesses a large number of migrant arrivals.

blocks.caption: The Red Cross is providing medical help and assistance to the migrants arriving in El Hierro (FILE: November 11, 2026)Image: Borja Suarez/REUTERS

blocks.text: "The Government of Spain continues to work to ensure that this surge in migration is managed with humanity and with the island's residents in mind," she posted on X. El Hierro has a population of nearly 12,000 people.

Although the Canary Islands a large number of migrants arriving on its shores over the weekend, overall migration to the islands is down 5.5% between January and October 31 from the same period last year.
Canary Island arrivals surge come after recent Ceuta crisis
The surge in latest arrivals to the Canary Islands comes after another Spanish territory, Ceuta, faced a migration crisis in late July.
Meet the woman feeding 100s of Ceuta's migrants

An estimated 80,000 people, mostly young Moroccan men, crossed into Ceuta from neighboring Morocco. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, a member of the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE), has faced criticism from the opposition over his handling of the crisis.
Migration, along with housing, are expected to be major topics for voters as they head for snap elections in Spain later this month.

articles.title: Zelensky urges US and Musk to lift Starlink restrictions and be on 'right side of history'
articles.summary: The Ukrainian president says restrictions are still in place and making it difficult to stop Russian attacks.

blocks.text: Ukraine uses the normal Starlink service for communications on the battlefield, while Starshield is used for the interception of missiles and drones in Ukraine airspace.
The issue of speed restrictions was first identified in October. It led to conflicting accounts by both Elon Musk and US President Donald Trump.
Musk said the US government was responsible as Starshield was controlled by them, but Trump denied being responsible and said he had told the billionaire owner to "put it back".
It appeared to be returning to normal after a week, following which Ukraine said the restrictions were still being implemented.
The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic stand-off between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.
Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, had pushed global prices higher.

On Sunday Zelensky said Ukraine was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones targeting electricity substations because "restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there".

"Our interceptor drones lose connection with their operators at a speed of 161km/h (100mph) and simply cannot catch up with Russian jet-powered 'shaheds'," he posted, referring to the drones that follow an Iranian design.
Ukraine has also been beset by a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors used to defend against Russian missiles - a situation that Russia has exploited to intensify strikes on Ukrainian targets.
Overnight and into Sunday morning Russia hit energy infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia and the Sumy, Odesa, Zhytomyr, and Kirovohrad regions, Ukraine said.
It also struck railway infrastructure in the Dnipro, Kharkiv, and Zaporizhzhia regions.
Scores of people are said to have been hurt in those attacks, as well as two in the Donetsk and Kyiv regions.
Two people were killed in an attack on an infrastructure facility in Chernihiv Region's Mena, governor Vyacheslav Chaus said.
Multiple strikes were also delivered on energy facilities across the region, he added on Telegram.
Ukraine meanwhile said it had carried out strikes on a petrochemical plant and an oil refinery in the central Russian city of Nizhnekamsk.
"On the night of November 15, units of Ukraine's Defence Forces reached Nizhnekamsk in Tatarstan," the military said on Telegram.
"Two enterprises that feed the Russian war with raw materials and fuel came under attack."
Other Ukrainian strikes killed one person in Taganrog, an industrial port city near the border, regional governor Yuri Slyusar said.
In the occupied Luhansk region a lorry driver and an elderly woman were also killed, Leonid Pasechnik, the regional leader installed by Moscow said.
Meanwhile Estonia has announced it will shut its border crossing points with Russia from 1 December following a suspected sabotage attack on a defence company.
Eight people were detained over an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems.
The Estonian authorities say they had been ordered by Russia's GRU military intelligence service to try and carry out the attack. Russia has not commented.
"Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences," Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said.

articles.title: Iran launches drone attacks against US military base in Bahrain
articles.summary:
Strikes cast further doubt on peace talks between Tehran and Washington with increasing risk of escalation

Iran has launched drone…

blocks.text: Iran has launched drone attacks against a US military base in Bahrain, casting further doubt on peace talks between Tehran and Washington and raising the spectre of escalation.
Blasts sounded over the Gulf nation on Sunday in the second Iranian drone attack in three days in retaliation for US strikes in Iran.

Meanwhile, in Yemen, Iran’s Houthi allies advanced against pro-government forces in the south, opening a potential route to Aden. Iran also claimed that a mine sank an oil supertanker in the strait of Hormuz.
The developments deepened gloom about the chances of any diplomatic breakthrough in the region.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said they launched six drones targeting a US air defence radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base in retaliation for “hostile US actions”. Authorities in Bahrain said air defences intercepted the drones before they reached their targets.

At a press conference in Tehran the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said Iran would continue to respond to any military aggression by the US or other states. Asked if the latest strikes indicated a change in Iranian direction as negotiations with the US have stalled, he said Iran was “not waiting for anyone” and was focused on its security.
US forces have conducted a series of strikes against Iranian targets in recent weeks, including Qeshm Island in the strait of Hormuz.
Donald Trump last week called them minor strikes and said Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states had cautioned him against large-scale combat operations.

However, the president also said Washington was no longer seeking a deal with Iran and that he had instructed the vice-president, JD Vance, to switch his focus to alleged corruption and fraud in Democrat-run cities and states.
Vance – who blamed the Republicans’ loss of Congress in midterm elections on the Iran war – had requested a personal meeting with Iranian negotiators to discuss peace terms.
A conflict that began with joint US and Israeli attacks against Iran in February remains at an impasse, with the US maintaining a naval blockade and Iran its chokehold over the strait of Hormuz.

In a separate development, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed that two ships hit mines in the strait of Hormuz and that one, an oil supertanker with 2m barrels of oil, sank. The ships suffered “massive explosions and fire”, said the statement.
There was no immediate independent verification. The US military recently claimed it had cleared all mines from main routes through the waterway.
The strikes against Bahrain suggested Iran has decided on a tit-for-tat response to US attacks.

blocks.caption: The US Naval Forces Central Command headquarters building in Manama, Bahrain.  Photograph: Mcs2 John Benson/Planet Pix/ZUMA Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Bahrain hosts big US bases, including a forward base that was home to the US Fifth Fleet and US Naval Forces Central Command, operating as a central support hub for military operations in the Middle East.

Tehran repeatedly targeted the kingdom until September, when there was a lull in attacks. That ended on Friday when Iran launched drones against a US radar facility. US Central Command said it shot down two drones without any injury or damage.
The attacks on Sunday prompted sirens and alerts from Bahrain’s authorities urging residents to seek shelter.
“It’s exactly what I was hoping wouldn’t happen: Iranian attacks starting again, with all the worry and uncertainty that go with them,” resident Hayat Ibrahim, 65, told Agence France Presse.
Bahrain’s foreign ministry called the resumption of attacks “heinous aggression” and a flagrant violation of international law.

The kingdom rejected Tehran’s “flimsy pretexts and baseless claims” to target its territory, it said in a statement. “The kingdom also rejects the transformation of its territory into an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible for these attacks and their consequences.”
Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar condemned the attacks and expressed solidarity with Bahrain.

In Yemen, Saudi Arabia’s campaign against the Iranian-aligned Houthi rebels reeled when forces fighting on behalf of the Yemeni government retreated from the Bab el-Mandeb strait to defend ⁠Aden on the southern ​coast.

“The Southern Armed Forces announce the implementation of ‌a redeployment operation for its forces from Dhubab Airport and the Bab el-Mandeb area, west of Taiz Governorate,” the main military force fighting for Yemen’s government in the south said in a statement.
The admission signalled the apparent failure of a six-week government counteroffensive to drive the Houthis from the mouth of the Red Sea to secure a key oil route.
A Houthi missile strike near Aden killed people and wounded 12 near Aden, AFP reported, citing military and government sources.

articles.title: Cape Verde election: Jose Maria Neves set to win second term
articles.summary: Nearly two-thirds of the voters in the West African nation voted to keep President Jose Maria Neves in office, according to provisional results.

image.caption: Cape Verde's President Jose Maria Neves was expected to secure a new five-year termImage: Danilson Sequeira/REUTERS

blocks.text: Cape Verde President Jose Maria Neves won re-election Sunday with 63.8% of the vote, according to provisional results from the country's electoral commission.
The 66-year-old Neves was seeking a second term as leader of the West African archipelago, which is known for its stable democracy.
His main challenger was 61-year-old Joana Rosa Amado, a former justice minister who secured around 31.6% of the vote.
Four other candidates also contested the election.

Some 420,000 people were eligible to vote in the west African archipelago, with the election being watched by about 150 observers from the Economic Community of West African States, the African Union and European Union.
Cape Verde among Africa's most democratic nations
Cape Verde is made of ten volcanic islands located in the Atlantic Ocean about 600 kilometers (375 miles) off the coast of Senegal.

The island nation is known for its democratic stability and good governance, and its economy has been showing strong growth. The Mo Ibrahim Foundation's 2026 index on global governance has the country in third place of Africa's 54 countries, with only Seychelles and Mauritius faring better.

blocks.caption: Joana Rosa Amado, a former justice minister, made history as Cape Verde's first female presidential candidateImage: Danilson Sequeira/REUTERS

blocks.text: According to the World Bank, Cape Verde is an upper-middle-income country due to its growing tourism industry.
The challenges it faces range from social inequality, the islands' geographic isolation and the lack of traveling options between islands.
The increased cost of living, energy prices and youth unemployment also play a role.
Cape Verde's World Cup journey sparks national pride

articles.title: German economy returns to growth, so why is the country still worried?
articles.summary: The German economy is growing again, albeit slightly. However, economists warn that without reforms, higher productivity and solid public finances, a loss of prosperity and growing debt threaten…

image.caption: Experts predicted economic growth of 1.3% for 2026 and 1% for 2027, but it's not enough for Germany's ageing societyImage: Michael Probst/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Is Germany's economy back on the up? The answer to that question depends on your perspective.

At the 2026 Mechanical Engineering Summit in Berlin this week, the mood was sullen. "A year ago, I said here: We are angry. Today I must say: We are stunned," Bertram Kawlath, president of the Mechanical Engineering Industry Association (VDMA), said in his opening remarks on Tuesday.

The mechanical and plant engineering sector was the backbone of German industry for decades. It once employed more than a million people; now 15,000 positions are being cut every month. Production has shrunk about 20% since 2018.
Kawlath criticized the federal government's infighting and lack of reform, as well as what the companies consider a continued high bureaucracy and tax burden.
"[We are] stunned by the whitewashing in so many government statements. Stunned by the increasingly visible decline of our country as a business location."
Germany's economy is growing again — a little
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz promised quick reforms and a rapidly noticeable economic upswing when he took office in May 2025. A year and a half later, reality has caught up with him.

Merz's coalition of his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), its Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union, (CSU), along with the center-left Social Democrats(SPD), keeps running into trouble. In addition, there are crises and wars. The German economy is facing more headwinds than seldom before, Merz said in October at the German Employers' Day conference in Berlin.

blocks.caption: Earlier this week, economic experts gave Chancellor Friedrich Merz their  2026 report — and words of cautionImage: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Given the circumstances, small successes are even more meaningful. "A heartfelt thanks for the good news you bring," Merz said when he received the autumn report of the Council of Economic Experts in Berlin, which predicted economic growth of 1.3% for 2026 and 1% for 2027.
The economic experts have a German government mandate to independently analyze business activity and make recommendations for economic policy. Earlier this year, they were much more pessimistic.

"The German economy has recovered quicker than expected from the energy price shock sparked by the war in Iran," said Monika Schnitzer, chair of the expert advisory board, explaining the prognosis. "We see a significant economic recovery, driven by surprisingly strong exports and high government spending."

The chancellor, who celebrated his 71st birthday on November 11, spoke of "encouraging signals" in his address. "The economy in Germany is slowly on the rise again. Considering the many crises in Germany, it was not totally expected that we would manage that."
Why 1% growth is not enough
But these improved prospects do not change the long-term problems. An ageing society means the bills for pensions, health and caregiving are constantly rising.

At the same time, the number of working-age people who finance these services is sinking. That puts increasing pressure on the public purse. According to Berlin's financial planning, social welfare costs, defense and interest on debt will account for 80% of the spending in the federal government's budget.
What are the German government's pension, labor reforms?

"We must realize that in the long term the expected revenues in the federal budget will not be enough to cover the planned expenses," Schnitzer warned. The growth rates are far below what is needed to secure the same level of prosperity as previous decades in the long term.
"To grow out of this budgetary predicament, we would need levels of economic growth which we haven't experienced in Germany for the past 50 years," she said.

The government is currently in final deliberations over its 2027 budget; spending upwards of €555 billion ($615 billion) is planned. Because revenue won't be enough to cover it, the government is planning to take on more than €118 billion in new debt. Adding the debt-financed special funds for infrastructure and the military, the new borrowing adds up to almost €204 billion.
Could Germany lose its top rating?

The economic experts have warned that if Germany continues with this path, the debt-to-GDP ratio could rise to 100% by 2040. This ratio indicates how high the national debt is in relation to annual economic output. At the end of 2025, it was 63.5%.

Germany is the only country of the world's leading democratic industrialized nations (G7) to still hold a AAA rating, the best possible credit rating in finance markets. It signals to investors the smallest possible default risk for German government bonds. "I want it to stay that way," Merz emphasized.
Germany under pressure

However, taking on less debt will not be simple. "A reduction in debt-based financing presents policymakers with a consolidation task of historic proportions and will require tough decisions," said Schnitzer. The belt-tightening must, however, be designed to enable growth. Some recommendations include reducing environmentally harmful tax benefits — like the energy tax breaks for diesel fuel.
The so-called "mothers' pension", a pension subsidy for older parents, should be revoked, said the experts. Tax increases could become necessary in the medium term, for example with value-added tax.
"The burden should be shared fairly between generations and societal groups," Schnitzer said.
Merz wants austerity throughout Europe

According to the chancellor, the experts' message has been received. Solid state finances are an issue in Germany but also throughout the European Union. Merz said there needs to be a consolidation course, adding that politicians have a duty to the younger generation. Reforms are needed, especially when it comes to social security systems.
Young startups — Germany's next tech champions?

Economic researchers are setting their hopes on increasing companies' productivity. Put simply, productivity describes how much a company can generate with its employees, machinery and resources in a set time.
According to the Council of Economic Experts, there is enormous variation even within the same industries. In Germany, the top companies are up to five times as productive as the weakest enterprises.

If the less productive companies caught up, economic growth could increase significantly, it said in the report. "New technologies and business models could drive peak productivity and allow new highly productive companies to develop."
Germany needs startups, venture capital
But innovations need capital. It's here that the Ifo Economic Research Institute sees considerable deficiencies.

New evaluations show that German universities produce significantly fewer successful business startups than their counterparts in the United Kingdom or United States. For example, for every 1,000 students, about 14 venture capital-backed founders emerge from the vicinity of Stanford University each year. In Cambridge, the European leader, it's 3.5. In Munich, by contrast, it's only 0.5.

There continues to be an abundance of inventors and tinkerers in Germany, especially in mechanical engineering. However, the message from the industry summit in Berlin was that for renewed success, labor costs must come down. Suggestions included longer working hours and more flexibility for employers around job protection.

The intention was not to cut employees' wages and salaries. However, a new study by the German Economic Institute commissioned for the German Mechanical Engineering Industry Association showed that extending the working week by an hour alone would increase real gross domestic product by 1.5% in the coming five years.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: 'He lived and breathed it': NCAA football prospect from N.S. has died
articles.summary: A Nova Scotian who was set to play football at an American powerhouse college is being remembered for his exceptional talent and desire to get better on the field, but his happy-go-lucky and…

image.caption: Marcellus Young Casario, 18, had committed to attending the University of Georgia beginning next year and playing for the NCAA Division I football powerhouse. (University of Georgia)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia·New

A Nova Scotian who was set to play football at an American powerhouse college is being remembered for his exceptional talent and desire to get better on the field, but his happy-go-lucky and teddy-bear nature off of it.
Marcellus Young Casario, committed to Georgia Bulldogs, remembered for boundless energy, happy-go-lucky nature

A Nova Scotian who was set to play football at an American powerhouse college is being remembered for his exceptional talent and desire to get better on the field, but his happy-go-lucky and teddy-bear nature off it.

Marcellus Young Casario, 18, a Grade 12 student at a Georgia prep school, died Friday after a medical emergency. His father, Devin Casario, said his son hadn't been feeling well lately and had been experiencing some heart issues.

The six-foot-six, 275-pound defensive end who grew up in Halifax was set to graduate high school next month and begin attending the University of Georgia in January, a school that has produced many NFL stars.
"He lived and breathed it, and his work ethic was incredible," said Devin Casario. "He had [a] relentless motor and he was very, very coachable."
Former coaches say that while Casario's size, speed and strength were exceptional, his desire to get better is what made him stand out.
Marcellus Young Casario is shown in a photo from his time playing with Rabun Gap in Georgia. (Submitted by Devin Casario)
Chanuen Flint, a former coach and family friend, said that even at the age of six when Casario started playing football, his passion was evident.
"You just knew right away when he showed up on the field, he was all business. [He] had fun doing it, but he was there to play football," said Flint.
Early days

Colby Smith helped coach Casario when he played mites football, for kids who are seven and eight. He remembers the team playing in a halftime scrimmage at a Saint Mary's University football game. The children formed a tunnel to give the giant university players high-fives as they came out onto the field.
"I think from that very moment he knew where he wanted to be when he got older … I can remember the look on his face when they came out and he wanted to be part of that," said Smith.
Casario played minor football for teams in Halifax, Timberlea and the South Shore.
He left the province four years ago to attend a boarding school in Aurora, Ont., which played some of its games against American schools.
Marcellus Young Casario, shown wearing No. 50, always stood out for his size playing minor football in Nova Scotia. (Susanna Baard)
Marcello Lio, the head coach at St. Andrew's College, coached Casario for two years.

"Sometimes it’s easy for a young man, maybe not as passionate, to walk away from a loss, accept it and move on," said Lio. "He had struggled with that, so he always had the will to want to be better individually and want the team to win."
Overcoming adversity
Casario attended Rabun Gap-Nacoochee School, a Georgia prep school, for the past two years. He had a hip labrum injury last year that required surgery and a six-month recovery.
It wasn't clear whether he would return to full form.
In August, when training camp began, Devin Casario remembers getting a call from his son, who was in tears.

"I thought something had happened," said Devin Casario. "But there were tears of joy because I really think his self-belief and faith were tested after that recovery process. And I think after that first night during the conditioning test down there, he knew that he was going to be OK."
Marcellus Young Casario is shown in his senior class photo. (Rabun Gap-Nacoochee School/Facebook)
The University of Georgia wasn't Casario's only suitor. There were visits to Michigan State and Georgia Tech, all of which are well known for their football programs.
Lio said he wasn't surprised that Casario chose the University of Georgia. There were other schools where he might have been able to get on the field sooner, but the Bulldogs offered something else.
"He wanted to be pushed; there was some yearning inside him to be constantly pushed hard to be the best he can be," said Lio.
During the past two summers, when Casario returned to Nova Scotia when school was not in session, he helped coach Flint's younger son, who also plays defensive end.
Smith said Casario was always very respectful, continuing to call him "Coach" long after he was his coach.
"Even though he had these great accomplishments, he always remembered where he came from and always paid homage to all the people that helped him get where he is," said Smith.
Criminology studies
Devin Casario said his son planned to study criminology at the University of Georgia.
He said off the field, his son led a quiet life and his faith was very important to him.

"I hope something positive can come from this tragedy, and that he can serve as an inspiration to other athletes who have dreams, you know, coming out of Nova Scotia and the East Coast that through talent and hard work, perseverance, anything is possible," said Devin Casario.
"And, you know, our family is destroyed right now and trying to make sense of this, but we're so proud of him. And it's just so unfortunate that his life was cut short."

articles.title: Despite restrictive abortion laws, Poland's 'Abortomat' — a locker that dispenses abortion pills — helps women who want to end a pregnancy
articles.summary: Abortion laws in Poland are very restrictive. Activists there have found a new way to help women wanting to terminate a pregnancy: the "Abortomat," a locker that dispenses abortion pills. But they…

image.caption: Polish activist Justyna Wydrzynska helps to operate the 'Abortomat,' a locker that allows women to access abortion pills swiftly and anonymouslyImage: Adam Easton/DW

blocks.text: Women's rights activists in Poland have opened what they say is the world's first delivery locker supplying abortion pills in a country with one of Europe's most restrictive abortion laws.

Known as the "Abortomat," the locker is in a building opposite the Polish parliament, in what activists say is a clear message to politicians like Donald Tusk. The Polish prime minister pledged to introduce abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy before the 2023 parliamentary election, but his coalition has been unable to agree on a common position.
Only two European Union member states, Poland and Malta, do not allow abortion on request.
In Poland, abortion is only allowed when the pregnancy is the result of a crime — rape or incest — or when it endangers the health or life of the woman.
Pink lockers and PIN codes

Justyna Wydrzynska, an activist from a nonprofit organization called Abortion Dream Team, showed DW the "Abortomat" in a small room behind a tasseled portiere at Abotak, Poland's first abortion center.

blocks.caption: Abotak, Poland's first abortion center, is situated opposite the Polish parliament and houses the 'Abortomat'Image: Adam Easton/DW

blocks.text: Inside, the pink lighting is subdued. Glitter tassels, baubles and spotlights make it feel a bit like a disco, she said.

The "Abortomat," which opened in late September, has 22 pink lockers. To open one, a woman receives a PIN code from the organization Women Help Women after completing a medical questionnaire, which is then checked by a doctor.
Parcel lockers have sprung up like mushrooms after rain in Poland in recent years. Even the smallest villages have them.
"When you walk around Poland, vending machines are everywhere. This is our culture. People in the US have Amazon, we have vending machines for everything," said Wydrzynska.
Convicted of helping a woman to have an abortion
Women in Poland who have an abortion are not criminalized. But anyone who helps them terminate a pregnancy risks up to three years in prison.
In 2023, Wydrzynska was the first activist to be convicted in Poland of helping a woman to have an abortion by sending her pills. The conviction was later overturned, and the court ordered a retrial.
'Abortomat': World's first abortion pill-dispensing locker in Poland
Inside each compartment at the "Abortomat" is a package that normally contains two drugs, mifepristone and misoprostol, usually taken up to the 14th week of pregnancy.

Because mifepristone is not registered in Poland, the drug must be ordered from abroad where it is legal. Information on how to do this is not easy to come by, which is where Abortion Dream Team and Abotak come in. They help women find information about accessing medication, which is sent from abroad by Women Help Women, or help them to travel abroad for a termination.
A 'complicated' legal situation
Wydrzynska said she believes the "Abortomat" does not break the law because it is a machine, not a person, that is delivering the pills, although she admits she is not sure.
Dr. Sabrina Mana-Walasek, a reproductive rights lawyer representing Wydrzynska, said the legal environment for abortion pills is "complicated."
She said that although mifepristone is not registered in Poland, it is registered in the European Union and, as EU citizens, Polish women can order it and take it.
"If a woman orders pills for herself and pays for them herself, it's not a crime," she said.
Opposition from Catholic groups
The ultra-Catholic legal group Ordo Iuris disagrees and has notified the prosecutor's office that the activists are committing a crime.

"In the case of an 'Abortomat,' the actions enabling a woman to have an abortion are theoretically performed by the woman herself using the device, but the reality is that this machine is operated by people — they send the code required to open the compartment containing abortion pills, they order and procure the pills, and they restock the compartments," said Katarzyna Gesiak, director of the Ordo Iuris Center for Medical Law and Bioethics.

blocks.caption: Comforting messages can be seen inside the Abotak center Image: Adam Easton/DW

blocks.text: Wydrzynska said anti-abortion activists regularly demonstrate outside Abotak, using horns and loudspeakers to generate loud noise to annoy the center's residential neighbors and pressure the landlord to revoke their rental agreement.
At one demonstration, a woman holding an image of the Virgin Mary told DW she believes abortion "is the work of Satan."
"Abortion is evil, it's demonic, it's against the fifth Commandment, 'Thou shalt not kill,'" she said.
Support for women seeking an abortion

Earlier this year, Diana, a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman living in Warsaw, used abortion pills during her sixth week of pregnancy before the "Abortomat" started up. She got the pills using information provided by Abortion Dream Team.
Diana told DW that she has never wanted to have children.
"I was expecting something like a headache, stomachache, maybe vomiting, but I had nothing like that. It was just like a normal period. I didn't feel any pain. It was really easy for me," she said.
"I felt relief because I knew that it was the right choice for me. I knew that I can live my life," she added.

blocks.caption: Before receiving a PIN code for the locker, a woman first has to complete a medical questionnaire from the organization Women Help WomenImage: Adam Easton/DW

blocks.text: Another Abortion Dream Team activist, Natalia Broniarczyk, said they help about 130 women daily in Poland. About 125 of these women use pills that cost about €75 ($83), while the remainder travel to a clinic abroad.
In contrast, just 851 abortions were performed in Polish hospitals last year.
Rising support for right-wing parties
Broniarczyk is concerned about the rising support for right-wing parties ahead of next year's parliamentary election, but she's also furious at the inactivity of liberals in Tusk's coalition.

"I'm mad at the liberals because for three years, they did nothing to protect us. They lost three years and now, when we're close to an election, they are fighting for our voices and respect. People are more progressive than politicians," she said.

After taking office in 2023, Tusk's coalition, which includes left-wing and conservative partners, were unable to agree a common position and their separate bills failed to obtain parliamentary approval in 2024.

blocks.caption: Natalia Broniarczyk believes Poland's president, Karol Nawrocki, will use his power of veto to block two bills recently passed by the country's parliament that would make abortion more accessibleImage: Adam Easton/DW

blocks.text: Afterwards, Tusk said abortion on request would not be possible during the current parliamentary term.
Two bills approved by parliament
In October, however, two bills were resubmitted to the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, and were narrowly approved.

One reinstates severe irreversible fetal defects as a justification for a legal termination. This justification had been ruled illegal by the Constitutional Court in 2020 when the previous right-wing Law and Justice (PiS)-led government was in power.
The 2020 ruling led to tens of thousands of people, mostly women, taking part in street protests in towns and cities across the country, some of the largest since communism fell in 1989.
Lawmakers also approved a bill partially decriminalizing anyone who helps a woman terminate her pregnancy.

According to the results of a recent poll conducted by SW Research for Onet.pl, almost 61% of respondents said they want the country's right-wing president, Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, to sign into law the bill on the fetal defect justification.
Nawrocki opposes abortion, and both Wydrzynska and Broniarczyk think he will use his power of veto to block the bills, preventing them from becoming law.
